subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO TREATMENT OF PERSONS DETAINED BY MOUNTED POLICE

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): I should like to communicate to the house a report I have received from the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police with respect to the treatment afforded the persons who were detained at Rockcliffe for interrogation by the .royal commission appointed to inquire into the so-called spy activities. It is dated March 20, 1946:
Dear Mir. St. Laurent:
. With reference to Mr. 'Caldwell's statement in the House of Commons on March 18, in respect to the persons detained in the present espionage inquiry iat Rockcliffe being accommodated in rooms which were brilliantly lighted and in which the lights never were out, the following particulars are submitted for your information.
On the occasion of the detention of the individuals referred to, in view of the fact that they had to be kept incommunicado, it was necessary that each .have his own 'personal guard so as to prevent them from conversing with other persons detained and also as a safety measure to prevent escape.
Official Secrets Act

Certain of the persons detained were given accommodation, individually in large rooms measuring approximately 60 feet by 22 feet, *while others were placed an small! .rooms, approximately 10 feet by 9 feet am measurement, due to no other large rooms .being .available. The small rooms .are those allotted to sergeants of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and are comfortable. As there is no proper cell accommodation at Rockcliffe .barracks, it was necessary that police guards remain in the room with the prisoner throughout the hours of daylight and darkness; consequently, it was necessary that a section of the room 'be lighted >at night, as the guard was not permitted to sleep. These were the normal lights installed for the rooms in question, but after the first few nights were replaced by a shaded reading lamp. Any charge that brilliant lights were installed in any of the rooms is not only untrue, but ridiculous.
AH those detained were treated exactly alike in all respects, and were given exercise daily in the company of an escort.
The complaints mentioned by Mr. Coldwell, M.P., and Mr. Solon Low, M.P., .are denied by two or more of those who were detained, as indicated by the attached^ press reports. No undue pressure or what is known as "third degree" methods were employed by the police, and there was no occasion, or reason for .any unauthorized treatment.
The meals served were those prepared for members of the force, under the supervision of <a dietitian. #
Yours faithfully, *
(.Signed) S. T. Wood,
.Commissioner.
The first clipping annexed- to the report, and referred to in the report, is from the Montreal Standard of March 16, 1946:
"Third-Degree" Grilling Denied by Spy Suspect Special -to The Standard
Ottawa, March 16-One of eight espionage suspects who had been held incommunicado for nearly a month at the R.C.M.P. barracks at nearby Rockdliffe told the Standard to-day that no third degree methods were used in questioning him.
This suspect, now at liberty on bail, refused to -allow himself -to be quoted by name on the advice of his lawyer. Otherwise he talked freely.
"If any coercion was used, it was of a most subtle nature," he said. "There was no physical discomfort-just adroit questioning by the mounties."
He spoke of his own experience only, but believed .that his treatment was not substantially different from that -accorded twelve other persons held in the police -barracks. Eight of these, including the Standard's informant, were -arraigned in court this week and freed on bail.
(Last week an unnamed -lawyer representing one of the detainees said the Mounties were using coercion- -and third degree methods to extort confessions, and -that his client was confined to a "stuffy little room- in which a bright -light was left burning continuously." R.C.M.P. Assistant Commissioner H. A. Royal Gagnon immediately -denied the third degree and coercion -allegations.)

"I was treated quite decently," the Standard's informant sa-id. "Even the guards were respectful-they called -me 'Sir.' We were confin-ed one to a barrack room, and I had practically everything I wanlted-^my sun -lamp, my pas-teils, all my own clothes, good food -and use of the barracks recreational library.
"Wh-at I disliked most was that I wasn't allowed newspapers, was -refused permission to see any visitors, even -my wife, ajnd that I was held d.ay after day with no charge being placed against me.
"My room was a large one, usually used as a dormitory for a number of policemen -attending courses at Rockcliffe. I had it all to myself, but I was never alone in i-t. There was always a guard with -me, -and at nig-h-t only the lights in the half of the -room in whi-ch I w-as sleeping were extinguished."
The constant guard -and lights were -believed to -be precautions -against any of the detainees attempting suicide. The Standard's informant said he was allowed possession of -a safety razor only while shaving in the morning, -and then only with -a guard near. He was allowed to keep his belt -and shoe laces.
"I was taken ou-tside the building for a walk each day, but my only companion was a policeman. Occasionally, I could see other civilians .through my window -taking similar walks under guard. I recognized two of -them, but was unable -to speak to them."
"The adroit questioning" by police was conducted by Inspector Harvison of Montreal, he *said. All questioning by the Royal Commission w-as oon-iucted in the Justice building, to which the Standard informant was taken by police.
He protested strongly against what he described as -the -injustice of holding -a person for weeks without allowing -him to see a lawyer. He said that when he was -arrested he -asked his wife to engage legal counsel but that -the lawyer was -not allowed to see -him.
It was only after the commission had finished questioning him that he was given the opportunity of call-ling in his lawyer, he asserted.
The other clipping is from the Ottawa Evening Citizen of March 6, 1946, but it does not purport to be a report from anyone who had been detained. It is merely a statement made by someone who had been retained as counsel for a person who had been detained. I do not think I should read it to the house as being pertinent to this question.
If I may be permitted to do so, I will table the report with the clippings annexed thereto.

Mr. Speaker, the-question as to a reduction in postage rates on gift parcels to the United Kingdom has been raised by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce), the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), and by members of the general public. Because this subject is one of general interest, I am making a brief statement at this time.
The present parcel post rates to the United Kingdom are fixed in agreement with that country, and are therefore not entirely under the control of the Canadian Post Office department. They consist of the, actual dost of handling in Canada, conveyance by ship, and the charges which are handed over to the country of destination for delivery costs. For instance, in the case of a gift parcel for the United Kingdom weighing the permissible limit of 11 pounds, and one cubic foot in over-all size, we pay 75 cents for sea conveyance and 90 cents to the United Kingdom, leaving Canada only 40 cents to cover all handling costs here, including rail haul.
Any reduction of these rates Vrould mean in effect a subsidy to the senders. There may well be an objection to this which I present for the consideration of the house. It is that the sending of gift parcels is a matter between individuals on the chance happening of a person overseas having a friend or relative in Canada. Government assistance should, I believe, not be granted on this narrow basis. Rather we should continue as at present to provide relief to those in need through official agencies operating for that purpose.
If the United Kingdom authorities wish to confer the benefit of reduced charges to their own people, we should be happy indeed to pass on to the Canadian mailers the reduced postage rates thus made possible. There has been no such disposition, however, on the part of the United Kingdom postal authorities. Recently when they were approached as to the possibility of accepting less than they now require for the handling of parcel post parcels, they pointed out that their charges are at an absolute minimum, and with rising costs at the present time they might even have to increase the charges which they now require.

A comparison has been made with the rate charged for soldiers' parcels. May I point out that these parcels were handled, from the time of mailing to the time of delivery by the Canadian postal service and the Canadian postal corps. The conditions were, therefore, quite dissimilar to those prevailing in the case of civilian parcels.

speechtext:
Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Secretary of State) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 7, re-specing citizenship, nationality, naturalization and status of aliens.
He said: The house will recall that on October 22 last I introduced a similar bill, and asked for first reading. My remarks, in which I set out the purpose and intention behind the bill, are found at page 1335 of Hansard.
The measure to which first reading is now sought, with some slight editorial revisions, including a definition of " domicile," is the same as that introduced last year. On that occasion the definition of "domicile" was left as interpreted in the Immigration Act.
A further provision in the bill now presented to the house is that it affords to members in the armed services the prerequisite of having spent only one year in the country, as a condition to their becoming citizens under this new legislation. So that for all practical purposes under the bill now before the house a member of the armed forces will almost automatically on application, subject to other qualifications, be eligible without going through the residence requirement for admission into Canadian citizenship.
As I stated on a previous occasion, an attempt is now made to give a new definition to Canadian citizenship and to clarify the ambiguity which follows from the Canadian Nationals Act, the Immigration Act and the Naturalization Act. The underlying purposes of the bill are really two: first, to achieve a clear and simple definition of Canadian citizenship which will remove the complexities which exist in the present legislation and, second, to provide an underlying community of status for all our people in this country that will help to bind them together as [DOT] Canadians.

And if we ask who is responsible for this state of things, I would say credit is to be given to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who has so well administered the department during the time he has been in charge of it.
In closing I would refer again to what I said yesterday with regard to the leader of the Liberal party, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King). Canada is indeed fortunate to have at the helm at the present

The Address-Mr. Diejenbaker
time the present Prime Minister-fortunate both in its domestic affairs and in its international ramifications.
Oh, oh.

I shall come to the criticism after a while. I was saying that I am not here to criticize the need of Canada to prepare for markets in Europe and elsewhere and to aid Britain during her dark days and reward her in part for what she did for us when she saved civilization. The farmer believes, properly I think, that if Canada intends to advertise, if Canada's government intends to secure markets abroad, then it should be done at the expense of the Canadian people and not at the expense of the farmers who produce the wheat.
One problem which faces the country was accentuated the other day when I visited Chatham; I refer to the necessity of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) doing something immediately to assure the necessary labour supply for the Canadian farmer.
That is something you should look after. You may be on the farm yourself.

Well, Mr. Speaker, let me tell you that there is never any fear of the genial Minister of Labour moving anybody around like that if the record of the past is to be any augury of what will happen in the future. When i was in Chatham I found that many of the farmers had been on sugar beet production, others on vegetable production. But these farmers, by reason of the failure of the government to face this situa-
The Address-Mr. Diejenbaker

tion acud to assure them the necessary labour supplies, are unable to determine what to do this summer. While the minister says that things will be bad for some of us in the future, the farmers in the county of Kent and in the part of Ontario to which I refer, are asking that a decision be made now, not on April 1 or April 15 or later, because, notwithstanding all the unemployment in the country, it seems impossible now to secure men who will return to the farm and assist in that kind of work.
What I am about to say applies p&rticularlj'' to western Canada. During the war a tax of three cents a gallon was imposed on gasoline with a view to discouraging its use. This tax added to the cost of the farmers' production. Why was it not removed immediately upon the conclusion of the war? Instead of the tax being removed, permission was given to the great western oil corporations outside the city of Winnipeg to increase their prices by two cents a gallon, effective during the present months.
I represent a rural constituency. I visited farmers everywhere in that constituency during the recess and I find they are willing to work in order to meet the challenge that faces the world. But, as the hon. gentleman who has just spoken has said, unless they are assured that longer hours will not penalize them in income tax, the production that is asked for now will not be obtained. If the government will not consider it proper to provide a real inducement in the form of relief from income tax for the extra production, what must be done is to increase the income tax exemption to the extent of $2,000 for married persons and $1,200 for single persons. In the second place, I suggest that while a great deal of wheat has been sold1 at $1.55 a bushel, the farmer should be given the reasonable price of $1.80 for every bushel of wheat sold since August 1, 1945, to the end that, by means of that encouragement, the production we ask for will be forthcoming.
The farmer is most insistent that he be given assurance of a market, and that he be given equality for agriculture, to use the expression of my leader; that by means of a well organized programme he be given security in prices several years ahead. I suggest that even at this time the government should turn its attention to these two matters-first, the provision of labour, not a month or six weeks from now, but immediately; and second, that the government give some hope to the farmer and to the other 
citizens of Canada of some relief from high income tax through an increase in the amount of exemption.
Having dealt cursorily with these two questions I come now' to the spy situation. I do not think there is any place better fitted for the discussion of this subject than the parliament of Canada, which, if it is to discharge its responsibilities, must be the bulwark of the liberties of the Canadian people. I am going to ask my hon. friends in all parts of the house to listen to the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, delivered in the House of Commons on March 19, 1918, words which I can never hope to emulate, setting forth the responsibilities of members of parliament in the determination, and in the securing and maintenance, of those rights which are dearer to no one than they are to people of British birth, dearer than life itself. Sir Wilfrid used these words:
Eternal vigilance is the price of- liberty, and the universal testimony of history is that unless *there is eternal vigilance on the part of a strong and resolute opposition-, encroachments upon freedom and abuses in office will creep in, just as surely and just as certainly as weeds and tares will invade and choke the crops of the husbandman if he is not constantly on v'ateh. Nay, more, I think I can invoke also the testimony of the history of British institutions to show that -if at any time there is on the part of some section of the opposition a relaxation in vigilance, weeds -and tares -at once appear in luxurious growth.
These are pertinent words, having regard to the encroachments that have taken place, during the period of the war, upon the rights of parliament:
Nothing, sir, is more certain than that one illegality will lead to another; that, -as a logical consequence, wrong will he followed by wrong.

It is strange, Mr. Speaker, that there should be so many interruptions in connection with a proposition as to which there is such universal agreement.
I was saying that I think I realize the situation in the world to-day. Stalin spoke on February 9; Kalinin spoke on February 4; Molotov spoke on February 4. They set forth the plan; and, according to the royal commissioners, here in Canada were men and women in the civil service wdio put their loyalty to a foreign ideology above their loyalty to the state. Anyone who runs may read the picture in the world to-day: Great Britain to get out of Greece so that the bases in the Dardanelles will be available; the U.S.S.R. demanding Tripolitania by way of trusteeship; the U.S.S.R. to-day in Iran;
U.S.S.R. asking for bases in Eritrea; the U.S.i, R. asking for the Kars plateau. It is a pictu. [DOT]* anyone can see; and the empire is not altogether guiltless when we allowed the U.S.S.R. to secure control over the Kurile islands, joint ownership or control of the Manchurian railway, the port of Darien and the port of Port Arthur, under the agreement at Yalta. tThese things exist; but, these things being recognized, and that spirit of communism spreading all over the world being known, it was passing strange for the Prime Minister to say he did not believe that Marshal Stalin knew anything about what was going on in this country.
I have no sympathy, sir, with those who would undermine their country in time of war or in time of peace. They are entitled 63260-10
to no sympathy, but they are entitled to be tried by law and not by administrative lawlessness. And let me say this. The Minister of Justice says the safety of the state is in danger. Nowhere in the orders in council does it say that, either in October or in February. It says, "it may be inimical" and all through Canada the press has taken the stand that the responsibility must rest with the government to prove to Canada that the destruction of these inalienable rights of British subjects is justified on the ground that there is in existence in this country a situation which would undermine the state and destroy our safety. It is well, too, to remember that as yet no one has explained the appointments made by this government. No one as yet has given an explanation as to why a Doukhobor woman from the constituency of Prince Albert, with a philosophy inimical to our philosophy, should come to Ottawa and find her way into the Department of External Affairs, where she would acquire a knowledge of our secret ciphers.
I might add that never in the long history of the British commonwealth has the "safety of the state" been defined as other than existed during a period of war, rebellion or insurrection. The minister says these are dangerous men and women. The authorities did nothing from September 5, 1945, to February, 1946; then they picked up these dangerous people and kept them ineomimfnicado for a period of time. Later these dangerous people were released on bail in trifling amounts which ordinarily would indicate the commission of no serious offence, and the probability of acquittal. If they were dangerous in January or February, are they not dangerous to-day? If they had to be kept under detention for that period, what has happened since to alter the picture? I say, Mr. Speaker- and it is not doctrinaire or a technicality- to say that these orders in council sweep aside Magna Charta, habeas corpus and the bill of rights. Some say the people of Canada are not interested in that. Sir, I do not believe the minds of liberty-loving Canadians, however much they hate communism, have become so apathetic in six years of domination by the state in a period when the political doctrines of regimentation inculcated by one party and practised by the other, have been in effect. I believe the time has come for a declaration of liberties to be made by this parliament. Magna Charta is part of our birthright. Habeas corpus, the bill of rights, the petition of right, all are part of our tradition. The United States has its own bill of rights, and I think out of the events of the last few years a responsibility falls upon parliament

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker

to assure that Canadians, as well as others in the empire and the people of the United States, should have established by their legislature a bill of rights under which freedom of religion, of speech, of association and of speech, freedom from capricious arrest and freedom under the rule of the law, should be made part and parcel of the law of the country.
During the period1 of the war of necessity parliament became a casualty of the war. We admitted that democratic symbolism and the leisurely processes of democracy had no place having regard to the tempo of modern warfare We voluntarily abrogated the rights of parliament and the rights of the individual, but I ask. the Minister of Justice to let us know his answer to this. If during the days of war he did not have the power he has under these orders in council, why was it necessary to apply to individuals in time of peace rules and regulations which were never applied in time of war? Section 21 of the defence of Canada regulations, which has been repealed by order in council, gave power to pick up aliens and enemies of the state during the period of the war. It gave the power of detention, but not the power of examination. Is this democratic symbolism? I defy the government to produce a case where during war, insurrection or rebellion when any British government acted not only to detain but to examine. As I look at what is taking place and what has taken place in recent years, this is what I am afraid of. Parliament abdicated many of its rights during the war, and to-day the government is endeavouring to perpetuate this temporary abdication. We placed our rights in pavra during the war as security for victory. To-day we are asking that those rights be restored to us and that parliament be assured of the prestige to which it is entitled by reason of our democratic development and the heritage that is ours.
This, as I see it, is the trend. From 1939 on, the government has arrogated to itself powers which ordinarily reside with parliament and the people. Indeed, during the period of the war there were the defence of Canada regulations; the present order in council goes much farther than the defence of Canada regulations did.
There has been an attitude on the part of the government denying us information. There was the philosophy of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) that the executive had no responsibility to parliament, the very antithesis of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had so often reiterated in the house.

And here is a strange thing: The minister says that on December 6, 1945, he did not remember this order in council of September, 1945 that swept aside Magna Charta and the bill of rights. He forgot itl Well, I accept his denial that he knew at the time of the existence of this order. But, sir, is it not an indication of what power will do to men, what it will do to a former president of the Canadian Bar Association, one who had stood for the safeguarding of the rights of parliament and the individual, that he should forget an order in council which did more to sweep aside the rights of individuals than has any other order in council passed in the history of Canada?
Parliament would never have passed the emergency transitional powers bill had it known about this order. But he forgot about that secret order! I wonder how many other secret orders the Minister of Justice has forgotten. How many other secret orders are there about which we know nothing to-day? I ask that question again, as I did on December 6.
Where is the rule of law? It is flouted by the government. First it is flouted by denial in many statutes and orders in council of recourse to the courts. True, most of those orders in council were connected with military needs. Why is recourse to the courts denied under certain legislation, such as that connected with the income tax and the excess profits tax, and a fundamental principle of justice, that a man may not be a judge in his own case, daily forfeited, to the detriment of business and of individuals across Canada?
Why does this government, which always asserted while in opposition that it is the custodian of the liberty of the individual, and yet denies to that individual the right of recourse to the courts-a principle of British justice since Magna Charta, which states, "To no man will we sell, to no one will we refuse or delay, right or justice."
When, in the history of the British empire, was any man ever denied counsel, except under orders in council passed by this government? Why deny counsel when an individual is brought in for examination? According to the statement read by the minister to-day there was no coercion. And, by the way, it was interesting to note that the Minister of Justice departed from his legal training to the extent of reading ex 'parte statements in a newspaper in order to support the answer he was gviing the' hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell).
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Will the hon. member allow me to make a correction? I was not

The Address-Mr. Diejenbaker
defending or supporting anything. I was indicating to the house the information I got from the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, which I had promised to get at the request of two members of the house.

Mr. Speaker, imagine the Minister of Justice giving information to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar as to wrhat the commissioner had read in the Montreal Standard, and then asking parliament to accept that as an answer!
You say I overdraw the story? What did parliament do a few short months ago in connection with a bill respecting emergency powers? Under the emergency powers bill, on October 5, 1945 the government endeavoured by order in council to get power to deport and to exclude Canadian citizens, or to revoke nationality. Parliament continued to sit until December 18. It would not accept the reactionary principle that a British subject could be deported at the will of the government of the day. Parliament, as represented by hon. members in all parts of the house, took the stand that such intolerance would destroy a nation. Parliament spoke on that occasion in words which could be understood by the government. Parliament pointed out that to deport Canadian citizens was the very antithesis of the principles of democracy, one of the first of which is that minorities are entitled to protection.
What did the government do? It could not get that iniquitous piece of legislation through parliament; so, while parliament sat, on December 15, 1945, the governor in council passed an order in council to do that which parliament would not allow it to do between October 5 and December 15, 1945.
There is the picture, as I see it. I cannot cover the various other infractions and invasions of democratic rights by the executive. I come back to the orders in council themselves, and I ask this: Having regard to the seriousness of the situation, why did the government let that order in council lie dormant from September to February? If it is so dangerous to-day to have individuals connected with the U.S.S.R. in this country undermining our state-and admitting it is-what was the justification for the government's allowing a Russian officer, Major Peter Domishev, to go to Churchill on the Musk Ox expedition, and there to take pictures of our equipment which will be used in the north country in the event of war's ever coming to this land? What is the justification for it? Surely not a fear of difficulties which in the event of refusal might arise between Canada and another nation, be-63260-10J
cause Canada and every other part of the empire is denied the same privilege in that country.
The only justification for these orders-in-council the government offers is that conditions are serious, and that it is done for the safety of the state. Sir, my answer to that is the answer I gave a while ago: detaining and questioning in this fashion has never been resorted to anywhere in this Empire before. I should like to know what would have happened in Great Britain, in the mother of parliaments, if the same condition had arisen. There, according to the Minister of Justice, one of the major wrongdoers, one of the alleged leaders, was not locked up for detention and examination. He was proceeded against by law and legal processes. After he had appeared in court, represented by counsel, he was denied bail, because invariably bail is denied when an individual may not appear for trial, or where it may be considered dangerous to allow him to be at large. Why was not the same practice adopted in this country? What difference was there here from the condition which prevails in Great Biitain. I suggest again that I have no sympathy for these people. I know none of their and never have. But are we not travelling along the trail which during the war was used and reused with an utter lack of protest on the part of parliament? This trail is becoming a highway along which the government moves, totally regardless of parliament.
The Minister of Finance said in a speech last fall that parliament's duty was not to scrutinize everything; it was to vote supply. That is the position that the government is coming to. It has taken away the right of the individual to have access to the courts. It has widened the defence of Canada regulations to the point where you say to the individual; Not only will you be detained to protect yourself and protect the country, but while you are detained you shall be examined; Is it not passing strange that these people are detained until such time as they say something which implicates them? They are then granted the right to have counsel; they are then permitted to face their trial. They are granted opportunity of freedom once they confess. When that happens they are withdrawn from the custody of the crown, from this so-called passive internment, and again have the opportunity to be at large.
As I said before, it is the first time in history that this has happened. Again I say that I have no sympathy for communists, but the great danger in the road taken is that if this becomes a precedent it may lead to
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker

caprice and personal animosity being the guide to prosecution of those who have different political views. These orders-in-council provide the government with a means whereby it may translate suspicions into proof by surveillance and the coercion of confinement.
My friend over there says that it works, that the end justifies the means. I have taken the trouble to look up the history of habeas corpus, and the more I have gone into it the more strongly I am convinced that the great and abiding principle of British law all through the ages has been a scrupulous regard for liberty. It was so even in the darkest days. To set aside those rights is to deny the foundation of British liberty. It works. The star chamber worked. It was efficient; it got convictions. There were outstanding judges at the head of the star chamber. But as McKeehnie says in his work on the Magna Charta, that writ is the principal bulwark of English liberty, and should the doubtful plea of political necessity lead men to look on its denial with apathy, the most distinguishing characteristic of our constitution will be effaced.
The orders in council provide a short-cut method, and so did the star chamber method. Maitland sums it up 'by saying that the star chamber probably succeeded, but it was none the less sinister. It too was composed of great jurists, but it became a court of inquiry, not a court of judges administering the law. Public opinion must be mobilized by knowledge against this practice. How apologetic the Minister of Justice was when he dealt with this matter; and I think the same thing can be said of the Prime Minister. Yes, it has been done before; parliament has been criticized before. None was more critical in the days before the war than the right hon. the Prime Minister. It may be said that to take a stand like this is not popular, but I assert that it is a member's responsibility to take a firm stand when he sees freedom being interfered with; when he sees such things as religious freedom being interfered with as it is when these Jehovah's Witnesses are still kept in alternate work; when he sees interference with the freedom of the press as was the case when certain photographers were advised that unless they delivered up their films they would be subject to arrest. When one sees that trend, when one sees bureaucracy not responsible to parliament, then the time has come when members in all parts of this house should rise and say that freedom and liberty are the concepts for which parliament must stand, that they will not permit the adoption by the executive of totalitarian

methods; that British methods have worked through the ages and British methods will work to-day.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, along with many other hon. members who have already spoken, I want to congratulate the two hon. members across the floor who moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Having done that, may I say that while I have taken part in many debates, I begin to feel a little nervous in taking part in this one. Since it has opened the discussion has taken us over a lot of territory. We have been chased by the police, taken into court, put into gaol, let out again on bail, taken over to Russia and also to several different parts of this country. It is therefore not without some diffidence that I rise to address the house.
I intend to speak in support of giving everybody in this country an equal opportunity, which is the first duty of government. I intend to base my submission, first, on a statement made by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King); secopd, on a statement of a former prime minister of Great Britain, and, third, on a statement of a business man in the United States. We can never attain the golden age of economic life while we are in the stone age of economic thought. I believe many of us are still in that stone age, and until we get out of it there is not much hope for the common man. Speaking in New York, on December 2, 1942, to the Pilgrims of America, the Prime Minister is reported to have said:
The only path to prosperity and peace is the path of equality of cooperation and of human brotherhood. The new order must be a world order. It must be governed by a universal rule of law. It m-ust be based on human rights and not on the rights of property, privilege or position. An end must be put to monopoly of power by any country and by any class.
That was reported in the Edmonton Bulletin of December 3, 1942. We have heard the Prime Minister tell us that we must have reform before the war is over, otherwise it will be too late. Late in December, 1940, former prime minister Churchill had this to say in London:
When the war is won, as it surely will be, it must be one of our 'aims to establish a state of society where the advantages and privileges which hitherto have been enjoyed by only the few shall be far more' widely shared by the men and youth of the nation as a whole.
I should like now to quote what a citizen of the United States said, Jesse F. Jones, a wealthy American who was formerly chairman of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation. He said:

The Address-Mr. Fair
These United States have been good to ns. We have made money, we have nice homes, wear good clothes, have fine cars and can afford banquets like .this one. We can look back fifty years when most of us started and chart the courses that followed. But we can't 'look ahead that far and see where we are going.
But there are some things we know about the future. One of them is that the days of making great fortunes are over. That is finished. Another is that the upper third, you and I, have got to have a more public-minded viewpoint. We must realize that the welfare and well-being of the lower third is our problem. We are as much of society as the fellow on the other side of .the tracks.
Many of us are wondering whether it is possible to have equality of opportunity until a thorough job of housecleaning is done in all departments of government and all other public institutions, where infiltrations of doctrines detrimental to our democratic way of life are to be found regardless of the label under which they operate.
Having laid that down as a basis I propose to say a few words about the millions of hungry people in other parts of the world. I was glad to hear the Prime Minister make his pronouncement on Sunday night last; and right here, may I say that I followed his injunction and went to church on Sunday, as is my regular practice, and I was wondering whether the Prime Minister used his Sunday morning in preparing his pronouncement of Sunday evening, or whether he went to church himself. His Sunday night speech was very good, and I am sure the farmers all over Canada received it in the proper spirit. I think you will all realize that farmers are necessary people at certain times, particularly when you want something to eat, and when there are taxes to be paid; whether they be exacted directly or indirectly makes no difference.
Speaking of cooperation, the farmers of Canada have had a lot of it in the past in the way of flowery speeches, but this time they demand cooperation in cash, not in credit or in words.
I should like to quote two paragraphs from the speech from the throne with which I propose to deal specifically:
Of world * problems demanding immediate action, the most pressing is the provision of food to those peoples facing 'acute shortage, .and, in some regions, widespread famine. The chance of a peaceful reconstruction of the world depends on food. The shortage at the present time is very great. The problem, moreover, is not only for the next few months, but also for the next few years. Unless the need is met, grave disorders, endangering peace itself, must fee anticipated.
The government is seeking by all practicable means to make available for export the maximum supply of foodstuffs. Every encouragement is being given .to increasing production.
The gravity of the situation demands, on the part of the people of Canada, -a united and wholehearted effort.
These words are clear and definite. I do not think anyone can accuse the farmers in any part of Canada of sitting back during the war years and not pulling their full weight in production. I cannot speak particularly for other parts of Canada, but I do know that in western Canada tractors were working night and day at certain seasons of the year on the farm; you could see tractor lights in the fields any night you were driving along the roads. For this the farmers deserve great consideration, The result of these long hours of work, about which we did not complain, after our able-bodied men and women had been sent into the services or into the civil service here or into munitions factories, leaving at home to work the farm men and women long past the age for such work as well as the young men who were physically unfit for the armed services, was that the farmers produced on a scale higher than they had ever reached before. I am not going to give all the credit for this to the policies laid down by the present government. It will be remembered that some years ago the Kaiser used to use the phrase ''Meinself-und Gott," and if we take into consideration the bounteous crops provided by Divine Providence during the war years, I think we would be hitting much closer to the mark.
Many of the farmers took the advice of the government; that is, they let it in one ear and out the other because they say that if you want to be a successful farmer you must do exactly the opposite of what the government advocates. In my own case I did not change my farming programme, and I do not intend to do so in the future, because if you are going to be a success on the farm you have to lay down your own programme, make sure it is a sound one, and then stay with it. If you are going to change according to every whim or faficy advocated by people who do not know anything about farming, you are not going to get very far beyond taking a walk down the road and letting somebody else have your farm. I do not think it would be fair to the government to deal with agricultural policy and the fate of agriculture prior to the time this government came into office. Let us take its wheat programme, starting with the 1935-36 crop.
It will be remembered that at that time we had an initial payment on our No. 1 Northern wheat at Fort William of 87i cents a bushel, and in addition we had participation certificates on which we were supposed to realize cash when the crop was all sold. That
The Address-Mr. Fair

continued for some time without prices getting any better; in fact, the price went down to 80 cents and then 70 cents a bushel, and at one time legislation was introduced to make 60 cents the initial payment on our wheat f.o.b. Fort William. The farmers of Canada did not like that. Perhaps it was done intentionally by the government so that the farmers would be thankful when the price was brought up ten cents a bushel through legislation passed in this house providing for an initial payment of 70 cents a bushel. That lasted until August 1, 1942. During this period, although we were getting a very low price for our wheat, we found that the prices of the things we had to buy were going up and up, and little attempt was made to check those increases. In addition, to taking the low price, because nature was good to Canada we were compelled to deliver on a quota basis. The farmers of Canada had no particular objection to that. They knew that a lot of our grain could not be used, and on one or two occasions we were paid some storage on the farms. But to most of us it was a case of buying lumber at highly inflated prices, building granaries and storing the wheat on the farms. Some of the wheat grown in the early years of the war still remains on some farms. On August 1, 1942, we had an increase to 90 cents a bushel. That served to compensate to a very small extent for the low prices which prevailed before that time. In 1943 the price was increased to $1.25, and in 1944 the quota was removed and we were allowed to deliver all the wheat we wanted to. In 1942, as I think we all remember, drastic changes were made in the income tax programme, and as a result farmers and others were compelled to pay income tax on income, in the case of a single man, above $660, and of a married man $1,200. There were some exceptions with which I will not bother at the present time.
In 1944, when quotas were removed, many people were carrying heavy loads of debt and paying thousands of dollars in interest, and they thought to themselves, "Here is my chance to get rid of my grain and pay off my debts." As a result many of them emptied and swept out their grain bins and felt that they were getting well away. Farmers, I may say, have at all times done their best to pay their debts, and on this occasion, having been compelled to pay interest on their debts and hold low-priced grain in high-priced bins, they took advantage of this opening of the quota and the increased price. In 1944 the war was still on, and farmers did not know at that time that they would be chased and compelled to pay income tax. But a short time ago, at the time of the Christmas and New

Year holidays, the farmers, at any rate around my part of the country, got some mail which was not very welcome. Letters were sent out containing income tax forms for the year 1944. Many of the farmers are still feeling pretty bad and pretty mad. Some of them stayed up at night trying to figure out their income tax. Thousands of them had not kept any track of their receipts or expenditures, and as a result they spent night after night trying to compute the tax as nearly as they could. In contrast to this, no effort was made by the government to visit the farmers in the depression years and find out what the losses were and try to compensate them or ease their interest rates, cut their debts or do other things of the kind. But after we had reaped, in ' 1944, one of the heaviest crops Canada ever produced, and in adidtion had delivered Surpluses which had been piled up as far back as 1940, the government came along and says in effect, "The war is over, we need money; and if the farmer has no extra money perhaps he will be easier to deal with." So they demanded their pound of flesh.
This is made the worse because farmers realize that in the past there was only one period, namely between 1915 and 1919, when the farmers of this country received their proper share of the national income-that is, about 33 per cent. In the depression years many of the farmers lost their farms and their health as well. During the war years I know of some cases-perhaps there were many-in which the farmer's wife got out and worked putting up hay, harvesting, and doing other farm work, and possibly a year later found herself in hospital undergoing an operation and paying doctor bills. This is not right. ' Something should be done to make conditions on the farm such that the farmer's wife and daughter will not have to go out and do farm work. But the help was not obtainable and the farmer's wife and daughter got out and did it, and they are still suffering as a result. Those who held on to the farms are still, even to-day, trying to pay off their debts and to meet the load of interest which in many cases runs up to 7 and 8 per cent. Why that is I do not know, because in many cases the amount on which the interest is paid is nothing but a book entry. This should not be allowed.
Farmers also are aware of the losses they have taken on grain in the past. A few years ago, at the time the price of wheat was raised to 90 cents per bushel, I took the trouble to figure out the number of bushels which were marketed between the 1935-36 and 1942-43 crop years, on the basis of the price obtained for it, and also what the farmer should have

The Address-Mr. Fair
received had the grain been sold at what has been called parity price, $1.41 per bushel. I might say that this parity is figured on the basis of farmers receiving 16-6 per cent of the national income, when they were really entitled to double that amount. According to the amount I arrived at, during that eight year period the farmers of Canada sustained on wheat alone a loss of $1,220 million. That sum would pay off a lot of farm debt and provide for homes, better equipment, better machinery and other improvements. But it has gone as a direct contribution to the life of Canada, for which the farmer has absolutely no credit.
Let me go back a few years. I am not accusing the present government with respect to these conditions; I am taking the period 1930-40. I find that the farmers during that period received a yearly average 9-4 per cent of the national income. If you include a few of the good years by taking the period 1926-40, you find that during that time the farmers received 11-3 per cent of the national income. In other words, approximately 33 per cent of the population of Canada had to be content with and get along on 11-3 per cent of the national income. If we take that wonderful year at the depth of the depression-1932-the farmers of Canada received five per cent of the national income. I think it is about time this government did something about it, and about time too that those of us here who represent agriculture and all other national interests got on our feet and made a demand, not a suggestion, that something be done about this matter right away.
In view of present taxation and price inequalities, what is the attitude of the farmer towards greater production? I have tried to point out the conditions under which farmers have worked during past years. All of you know what the present taxation programme is. The married rr\an, including the farmer, is supposed to be allowed an exemption of $1,200. Take for instance the man who gets $1,200 out of his grain and cattle or -whatever else he may sell, and in the past has undertaken to raise hogs. Probably the average small farmer will raise about sixty hogs. He takes those sixty hogs and sells them at $25 apiece, and when he comes to settle with the income tax collector he finds that he has to turn over the proceeds of the sale of twenty hogs, or one-third of his production, to satisfy the income tax demand, simply because he has worked many extra hours on production. In many cases he has had his tractor going twenty-four hours a day. And that is the thanks the farmer gets.
One of my neighbours visited me shortly before I came here and said he was worried about his income tax. He is a man I have known for over thirty years, and he has worked all that time for farm machine companies' and mortgage companies. In 1944, however, like many others, he took advantage of the quota on wheat and sold all the wheat he had in his bins using practically every cent of the money to pay off mortgages and machine company debts. Now he is faced with the problem of paying income tax on that. I couple of days before I left home he said to me, "Do something about this income tax in Ottawa, because I have to mortgage my land again in order to get enough money to pay the 1944 tax." That is the way in which the tax and price system operates to-day.
Some time ago we had an announcement that our wheat would be sold for export purposes at $1.55. I strongly protested against that. I do not want anyone to get the impression that I am not in favour of Canada giving wheat, at a good price, to Britain and other starving countries, but I do object to the farmers of Canada paying for the gift of the Canadian people. It is the gift of the Canadian people and the expense should certainly be borne by the Canadian people.
We were told that our wheat for export purposes would be sold at $1.55, but to make up for that we were also told that for the next four crop years our wheat would not be sold below $1 a bushel, f.o.b. Fort William. To the farmer in my part of the country that means 75 cents a bushel at the farm, and that is not nearly the price of wheat under present conditions. This again is government policy. Perhaps the government wants to get thanks from other countries; but again, as I said before, if it wants to get the cooperation of the farmer the government must pay in cash and not in credit or in flowery speeches.
It was announced yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the initial payment on this year's crop would be $1.25 a bushel. Under present conditions I am requesting, in fact demanding, of the government that they make that initial price $1.50, with participation certificates. World conditions to-day justify that price, and if there is to be a subsidy then it is the Canadian government's job, or the job of the people of Canada. Do not however continue to have the farmer make these gifts to other countries and bear all the cost himself. We are willing to produce the goods, and it is up to the government and the people of

during the week; on Sunday the mother goes home and does the housework, the house cleaning and the washing and so on, and goes back to the hotel Monday morning. This man has applied for old age pension, but because he has not been in Canada the full twenty years his application has been denied. I am not blaming any of the authorities; I am blaming the members of the House of Commons. It is our responsibility. Here we have in our midst a man who is not getting proper nourishment. I am not going into any further details, but this is only one of many cases I could relate.
We have too much food here; we cannot distribute it simply because man-made laws passed twenty years ago stand in the way. I wonder what is the matter with us. Are we all still in the stone age of economic thought? I am asking you, Mr. Speaker, to insist with me that these conditions must be changed so that our bounteous production may be made available to the people of Canada, and to the world after our own wants are supplied. There is a way, by which no man will be made poorer but by which the poor will be made richer. Let us adopt it.
Hear, hear.

It is understandable that some hon. members sitting behind the leader of the opposition feel that the housing problem could be solved, just like that- simply by marking one's ballot on election day, and by replacing one government with another holding exactly the same views.
No.

Let me remind the house that the leader of the opposition for twenty years was premier of Manitoba. However, he did not say the other day that much had been done during those twenty years to improve the housing situation in that province. From the dome of the legislative builds ings in Winnipeg it is possible to see some of the most disgraceful slums in Canada. I am not suggesting that slum conditions there are worse than anywhere else; but I have some pictures which disclose a pretty ugly housing condition in that city. Let the leader of the opposition tell us one thing that was undertaken to solve the housing problem of Manitoba during the term as premier. In Manitoba they have an abundance of cement and lumber, and they have a vigorous climate. They have all the factors that should result in the government on the provincial level facing up to the problem and providing some decent houses. My hon. friend suggests that the situation has grown worse, but I can show the house pictures of houses that have been occupied for some fifty years. They were occupied during the time the leader of the opposition was premier of Manitoba.
I do not wish to spend any more time in criticizing the government for what has been done. I think all hon. members will agree that this government must face up immediately to this problem and demonstrate to our people that we can do in peacetime the sort of thing we did in war time when we broke the bottle-necks that existed, when we established new records of achievement in every field of production.
I think the first thing we must recognize is that we shall have to have some plan. We shall have to work out some technique so that the federal government, the provincial government and the municipal government can participate. We have used the British North
The Address-Mr. Nicholson

America Act to pass responsibility from one authority to another. The result is that at the moment no level of government is taking the right type of action.	.
Thousands of our young people fought to save their homes. They have returned, and where are those homes that they fought to save? They cannot be found in Toronto, in Winnipeg, in Ottawa or in any city of Canada If you do not believe me go to the reading room and check the want ad section of the daily papers from coast to coast. You will find pathetic appeals by ex-service men and their wives who want living quarters. They would be satisfied with anything. Even though rewards are offered, housing is apparently not available. So that the first job is to have the federal authorities take the initiative of bringing the provinces and municipalities together to sit around a conference table and decide on a technique that will result in houses being built. We solved many complex problems during the war, and it should be possible to work out the necessary details in order to set up the administrative machinery and get action at all levels of government.
In the meantime I should like to suggest a programme which I think is feasible, a thirteen point programme. We have had many programmes containing different numbers of points offered, but I think this thirteen point programme in connection with housing should be launched immediately. My first point is that we should stop the unnecessary export of building materials. I followed with interest the statement made yesterday by the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe). He did not seem greatly concerned about the large export of Canadian lumber. I am sure that all Canadians are anxious that some of our lumber should go to rebuild Great Britain and war-tom Europe, but I would remind the house that that is not where the bulk of our lumber is going.
During the Christmas recess I visited California and I saw a great many houses under construction. Some of our finest Canadian lumber was being used. I am most anxious that we retain friendly trading relations with our good neighbour, but with our housing situation so acute I do not think our neighbours to the south would expect us to deny our people necessary shelter while Canadian lumber is being used for luxury building in the United States. I saw a great many houses under construction, but I do not think any of those being built would cost less than $10,000. Perhaps it is no business of ours what type of houses are being built in the United States, but surely it is a matter of

concern as to how much of our lumber is being exported and how much we are retaining for ourselves. The Monetary Times in a recent number contained a statement by the timber controller, as follows:
"No change has occurred in the quantities that will be allowed for export," explained Canada's timber controller, D. D. Rosenberry. "The only difference is that .producers now may ship that portion of their lumber to the countries of their choice."
In the. United States less attention is paid to price ceilings than in Canada or Great Britain, and the result is that higher bidders will take all the lumber we wish to ship and the companies shipping lumber in this country can select the country to which they wish to ship. I notice in the same article that W. J. LeClair, secretary-manager of the Canadian lumbermen's association, says:
If control were removed-within forty-eight hours we would not have one thousand feet .in this country remaining in our possesion-legally and financially speaking.
Surely it should be the concern of this government and our people that sufficient lumber should be retained here to do the job of building decent -houses for our people.
My second point is that we should prohibit deferable and non-essential building and stock-pile materials for housing construction.
Third, all building supplies in short supply should be rationed, giving top priority to housing costing under $5,000 per unit. Fourth, we should expand the .producfion of materials to meet an objective of 100,000 housing units in 1946: This would provide employment for at least 250,000 workmen and would cost approximately the same as our aircraft production programme of 1944. I realize the difficulties that would be encountered, but wihen we consider our performance in the field of [DOT] shipbuilding, aircraft production, tank production and so on, the building of 100,000 housing units in 1946 should be play compared with the difficult assignment carried out during the war.
Fifth, we should exercise better price control of building supplies and equipment until we make sure that there is enough material for all our people. In the United States congress there is now in committee stage a bill providing for ceilings on both old and new houses. In the original bill there was provision for $600,000,000 in the form of subsidies to keep prices within the reach of people who most urgently require accommodation.
My sixth point is that crown compaines should be set up to break the bottle-necks created by monopoly industry. As the Minis- [DOT] ter of Reconstruction told us yesterday, lumber

The Address-Mr. Nicholson
is not the greatest problem. We are short of plumbing supplies, electrical appliances, building boards and other' materials. During the war the government of this country found it necessary to establish crown companies when private concerns were unable or unwilling to do the job. The building of houses is a most important job for us now, and certainly some of the crown companies should be reorganized to produce materials in short supply.
My seventh point is that we should ensure the training of workers in the needed building skills. Again we take our pattern from the war years. We trained inexperienced young men and women from farms, towns and villages in welding, rivetting and all the essential jobs in our war industries. We now have a similar challenge, and our inexperienced people should be trained in the arts of house building.
My eighth point deals with the labour problem that would arise. Naturally men in the building trades would be concerned if large numbers were to come into the building trades on a temporary basis. We should enlist the cooperation of the men in the building trades by -assuring them that Canada is prepared1 to embark on a long-term extensive building programme. The Prime Minister referred to New Zealand. I have not forgotten the speech that the Hon. Walter Nash made when he was here during the early months of the war. Mr. Nash outlined the objectives of the Labour government of New Zealand in the field of housing and said it was their goal that every family should have a plot of land on which they could raise flowers -and vegetables, that every family should have a separate housing unit and that every individual should have a room where he could close the door and say: "This is my room; this is where my books and papers will be left, and when I return they will be exactly as I left them." Such a programme has never been enunciated or accepted by any government in Canada. We certainly -have done very little to see that that sort of ideal should be placed before the Canadian people. But if this government was prepared to say that Canada will use Canadian materials and Canadian working men to carry out such a programme, all the men in the building trades would be assured of full- employment on a yearly basis for an indefinite period.
My ninth point is that section 9 of the National Housing Act should be amended, if necessary, to give the provinces and the municipalities the right where desired, to establish limited dividend corporations -to engage in housing. It is obvious that the mortgage companies are not dealing with this problem as it should be dealt with, and where provinces
or municipalities wish to deal with this emergency problem they certainly should have the right to do so.
My tenth point is that subsidies should be provided to make sure that the difference between what the worker can pay -and what is economic rent should be bridged by some authority, and the federal authority is the one to make that gesture. It is recognized that a great number of people in every country do not normally receive a large enough wage or income to provide decent accommodation. I have here a little booklet entitled, "Planning the Canada of To-Morrow", written by Gordon McL. Pitts, president of -the architects' association. I find that according to these 1941 statistics 10 per cent of our Canad-ia^ workers received an income under $400. If you assume that they could afford for rent 20 -per cent of their income, that group should not pay more than $6.50 a month. Then 12 per cent received an inoome between $400 and $799, which would enable them to pay $7.30 a month in rent; 18 per cent received an inoome between $800 and $1,199, on which they could pay a rent of $20 a month; and 22 per cent received an income between $1,200 and $1,599, which would enable them to pay $25 a month rent. It also shows that 62 per cent of the population of Canada earned less than $l,6oC a year, none of whom could afford to pay more than $25 rent and, -as I have already pointed out, 10 per cert earned an inoome on which they should not be paying more than $6.50 a month rent.
Nathan Strauss, a pioneer in public housing in the United States writes in the "Seven Myths of Housing":
The public housing programme is foiunde-d on the fact that, without .government subsidy, decent housing cannot be put within the means of the families that live in . . . slums. This fact, distasteful as it may be to many people, is incontrovertible. History and mathematics both confirm -it. To achieve the goal of rehousing -those 'families, the -rents charged can be little more than half the -rents w-hic-h must be charged in livable new housing erected by private enterprise.	,
The federal Government is the only authority financially able to provide these subsidies.
My eleventh point is that Wartime Housing should be continued. In view of the criticisms I have made of Wartime Housing in the past it might seem strange at this stage that I want to see it continued. I frankly admit that Wartime Housing constructed and made available at lower rates better housing than the people who live in these quarters would have had if Wartime Housing had not come into the picture. However, I suggest that Wartime Housing, instead of building temporary houses which will eventually become
The Address-Mr. Nicholson

slums should build permanent houses. It is unfortunate that Wartime Housing regulations, certainly in western Canada, have insisted that basements be not allowed. But the difference in cost between temporary and permanent housing is so small that I suggest that nothing but permanent houses should be built. In Great Britain, with a very short supply of materials, it has been announced that it is government policy that permanent rather than temporary houses shall be built. This will result in fewer houses being available at the end of 1946 but on the other hand the people who are housed in them will have permanent homes and the materials will not be wasted.
My twelfth point is that the National Housing Act should be amended so that loans might be made up to the full cost of houses. I understand that at the present time it is very difficult in most cities to get houses built at the valuation; that a house which costs $7,000 is valued for lending purposes at, say $5,000. A house costing $5,000 is declared to have a rental value of $4,000, and consequently the prospective owner must advance $1,400 to secure a maximum loan of $3,600. The act should be amended so -that the prospective owner should not be required to make such a large initial payment.
My thirteenth and last point under this head is a recommendation that machinery should be established so that loans might be made available to farmers and residents of towns and villages under the National Housing Act. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) will probably reply that there is nothing to stop that now, but one of the returns brought down last year showed that not a single farm dwelling had been constructed in Canada under the National Housing Act.
I come to my next suggestion, which must be part of any over-all solution, namely that the provinces should be taken immediately into the confidence of the federal authority and the responsibility of each worked out, and then I suggest that the provinces should pass legislation defining the metropolitan and regional areas within the province. News items appearing in the Ottawa papers recently regarding disputes between the city of Ottawa and the township of Nepean indicate the problems that arise as we try to acquire land to solve our housing problems. The metropolitan cities in Canada or in any other country are a collection of a number of separate corporations, and if the housing problems of the people living in that area are to be solved there must be a larger unit that will have jurisdiction and authority to purchase land and plan and zone the communities.

The idea of planning our Communities is not a new one. In the days of the Romans the authorities worked out carefully prepared plans for their new communities. When they were establishing a new town they decided where the market should be, where the churches and the residences should be and what form of protection should be provided against a possible enemy. All these details were carefully worked out. But unfortunately in the building of Canada these factors have not been taken into consideration. In the building of our towns in the west, for instance, someone who owned some land and had some pull was able to get a townsite established on his section, and even though there might be good water and a good building site a mile away towns were frequently built on swamps or in the worst possible location. All this sort of thing results from the failure of the authority on the provincial level or on the national level to set up metropolitan and regional areas and plan their development. So that the job to be done by the provinces would be, as I see it, to make sure that they have their metropolitan and rural regional areas planned so that there may be an orderly development of the various communities within the province.
Other responsibilities of the province would be to set up limited dividend corporations and participate in the job of building houses, if necessary. They should allocate the dominion loans to the corporations and guarantee 'the repayment, and they should also provide for the building of houses in communities which have not been organized or in communities where the local commissions are failing to function.
A final word about the responsibility, on the local level of government, of the local authorities. Here is where the rank and file of the people must participate actively, in seeing that the slums are cleared, that the type of houses built are to conform with modem standards, taking into account our great resources and the type of housing we should like to have for ourselves and for our children. The local municipalities should appoint members to metropolitan or regional commissions who, with local members representing the provincial and federal authorities, would plan their areas, set priorities under the plan, buy, expropriate, hold and lease land, plan neighbourhoods, lease land for public housing, according to their over-all plan, and re-house those moved in slum clearance. It will be necessary, of course, for them to raise their share of the local funds required to carry out their programme.

The Address

Mr. Arsenault
In conclusion, let me summarize the responsibilities on each level of government.
Ottawa must provide enough building materials, must channel them to low-cost houses, provide funds for a large-scale housing programme, and make them available to provinces for low-cost, low-rent houses.
The provinces must promote the home building programme, co-operate with the dominion and the municipalities, set up metropolitan housing commissions, and help them plan and build neighbourhoods.
The municipalities must follow through on the local level, join the housing commissions to make them work energetically, and stimulate local interest and education for neighbourhood building.

Mr. Speaker, during the last session of parliament, a resolution was voted in this chamber, which read in part as follows:
Resolved, that in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that Canada possess a distinctive national flag and that a joint committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons be appointed to consider and report upon a suitable design for such a flag . . .
The joint committee appointed held two
meetings, on November 27 and December 4, 1945.
About fifteen hundred various flag designs were tabled before the members of the committee, who felt unable to formulate a specific recommendation in the short time at their disposal. A similar joint committee will be set up to continue the study of this important question at the present session of parliament.
Therefore the choice of a national flag for our country stands amongst the matters of major importance which will be dealt with by the members of this house in the course of the coming weeks. My intention in bringing this subject forward at this early stage of the session, and purposely before the flag joint committee resumes its work, is to give to this contentious but at the same time vital problem an entirely new approach, an approach which is not based on either English-Canadian or French-Canadian sentiment but merely upon daring logic. At the same time I am endeavouring to bring, in this important national issue, my modest but sincere contribution to national unity.
For many years there has been a growing sentiment in favour of a distinctive national flag in every part of Canada. Although a young nation, Canada finds herself to-day one of the important powers of the world. In the course of the last thirty years our country has performed great achievements from which Canadians derive a glowing national pride,
and this translates itself into a distinctive Canadian spirit. This new Canadian spirit grew to unexpected proportions during these last war years, particularly amongst our service men and women. As a result, never before in our history has there been a time when Canadians were prouder of being Canadians. And anywhere in the world where a Canadian may go to-day, he is welcomed, he is greeted, and he is highly respected as soon as he identifies himself as a Canadian.
Certainly the time has come when that Canadian, proud as he is of his own land, should be given a distinctive sign by which he could easily, promptly and fully identify himself at first sight as being a Canadian. The time is now due when this country, our country, should be given a distinctive national flag by which she could distinctly identify herself from other parts of the world, a Canadian flag that would make every Canadian boy and girl live, not for the country his or her ancestors came from, one or two or three hundred years ago, but live for, work for, fight for, and be ready to die for his or her own sacred native land-Canada.
Nothing has contributed more to the rise of sectionalism in this country in the past than the lack of a national flag, in Canada and for Canada. We need a national flag, distinctly Canadian, which will recall to all Canadians that their hearts should be broad enough to love their family, their village, their province, but above all, their Canada, a national flag which will infuse into the hearts and minds of Canadians a sound sentiment of duty and responsibility toward their land, all of their land.
Had we all been true Canadians in the past; had we steadily instilled the principles of Canadianism, without hyphens, without descriptive prefixes; had we "let the dead bury their dead"; had we had a distinctive national flag, then most of the differences which tend to divide us Canadians of different racial extractions, especially in periods of national emergency, would never have arisen.
At this point, may I recall that perhaps no individuals in Canada hold more power in their hands to spread about unity throughout this country than the representatives of the Ottawa press gallery.
Speaking from the experience which I have gathered during the last session of parliament,-may I add that in no other place in Canada have I 'found a more tangible and more sincere spirit in favour of Canadian unity than amongst our good friends of the press gallery. They can rest assured that their constant and valuable efforts in favour of bringing about
The Address-Mr. Arsenault

a better spirit of understanding in this country are widely recognized and highly appreciated by all true Canadians.
Other apostles of Canadian unity can also be found in the editorial rooms of many of our leading Canadian dailies, weeklies or periodicals as well as in the newsrooms of our broadcasting stations. To indicate to what extent the majority of Canadians of either language are able to agree on matters of principle pertaining to the government of this country, may I give as striking examples the editorials written day after day, and week after week, by two outstanding Canadian journalists. One is English speaking, the other is French speaking. One is Mr. B. K. Sandwell, editor in chief of Saturday Night of Toronto, whose editorials are widely welcomed in the province of Quebec as much as they are in other parts of Canada. The other is Mr. Eugene L'Heureux of Quebec city, who for many years contributed regularly to five daily newspapers in the province of Quebec. Mr. L'Heureux' daily editorials reflect the sentiments and the deep thoughts of the majority of the people of the province of Quebec, yet they could be translated and published in newspapers of English expression throughout Canada, and win the approval of most English speaking Canadians, as well as Mr. Sandwelks editorials could be translated into French and published in any newspapers of French expression and be well received by Quebec readers at large. What is the reason? Both are true Canadians, and represent each in his respective sphere the sentiments of all true Canadians of either language.
