From a letter sent out to the members of the Senate and the House of Commons in October last by the Toronto assembly No. 107 of the Native Sons of Canada, I quote briefly:
In a national flag if more than one emblem is displayed the upper lefthand corner next to the staff is reserved for the emblem of the dominant state, and the lower rightband comer on the fly is reserved for the vassal or subservient state.
A national flag speaks of the authority of the parliament of the country if represents. The union jack speaks of the authority of the parliament of the United Kingdom, and its inclusion in the place of honour in a. Canadian flag means that Canada is >a dependency of the United Kingdom.
May I quote now again, briefly, from an editorial published in the well known Toronto weekly, Saturday Night, on October 27, 1945, entitled, "Nation and Flag":
Surely the opponents of the official recognition of a Canadian, flag must see, if they will look at the matter with their brains and not with their feelings, that it is fundamentally absurd for nation A, which is so distinct from nation" B, that it can be at peace when nation B is at war and at war when B is at pfeace to insist that its flag and the flag of B are and must ever remain identical.
A national flag is a symbol of sovereignty. The sovereignty of Canada is vested in the Canadian people, as the sovereignty of the United Kingdom is vested in the people of the kingdom. They are not the same sovereignty. They do not need the same flag.
If there are any Canadians who should be entitled to have something to say about the choice of a national flag in Canada, I assume that this house will agree with me that they are those gallant, courageous and brave young service men and women who in this last war year after year-and they were long years- thousands of miles away from their native land were doing the fighting.
In the December 10, 1945 issue of the Canadian army forces newspaper The Maple Leal published in London, England, I read that service men speak out loudly for a truly Canadian flag. May I quote briefly:
Reported erroneously in ia Canadian dispatch as having been approved by the king as the national flag of Canada, but later found to be only one of a thousand designs submitted, the controversial banner incorporated a union jack in the upper lefthand corner, a sprig of three maple leaves in the centre of a white field and three golden fleur-de-lis on a blue circle in the upper right-hand corner. That the matter of Canada's flag is close to the heart of Canadians overseas is shown by the fact that more letters were received on this subject in the past two days than on any other subject or controversy over an ordinary two-week period.
Here is a short quotation from an editorial published in The Maple Leaf qn this subject entitled, "Ottawa Papers Please Copy":

Who has a better right to voice their opinion on the proposed all-Canadian flag than the men and women of Canada's fighting forces now being demobilized ?
Elsewhere on this page are excerpts from letters written by all ranks of servicemen and women of the navy, army and R.C.A.F. Almost of one accord they express a well-round "No" to the proposed flag, the sketch of which appeared in the December 6 issue of The Maple Leaf. We know that the story of this particular flag is not official, but it has served to uproot a flood of opinion that cannot be ignored. _
A recent Gallup poll resulted in sixty-eight per cent of the people in Canada wanting an entirely distinctive flag. And now the voice _ of Canadians in the United Kingdom is being heard in no uncertain terms. We believe that their ideas should carry as much weight as Canadians at home. To the committee at home in whose hands lies the final selection, we say . . . please note.
In this convincing manner the editor of The Maple Leaf supports the opinion of his correspondents on the flag issue. And I sincerely hope that every member of the house will carefully note the opinion expressed by our servicemen and women on the choice of the national flag, such as outlined in The Maple Leaf. With them I repeat:
Who has a better right to voice an opinion on the proposed all-Gandian flag than the men and women of Canada's fighting forces now being demobilized?
And I will add: Who knows better than they the meaning of sacrifice for country?
At this point I wish to make a clear distinction between a national flag, an official flag and an authorized flag or ensign. Canada has an authorized ensign and an official flag. Canada has as yet no national flag. Canada has had an authorized ensign since 1892. That is the red ensign with the Canadian coat of arms in the fly which was authorized for use by merchant vessels registered in Canada. That was confirmed by the Canadian Shipping Act of 1934.
Canada has had an official flag since 1911. The union jack was officially declared to be the proper flag to be flown on land in Canada. I cannot think of any reason, historical, constitutional or otherwise why the union jack and the red ensign should not be retained in their particular places to fulfil their particular functions, one as our king's flag and the symbol of our membership in the British commonwealth of nations, the other as the ensign of our merchant ships, with perhaps a maple leaf in the lower right-hand corner instead of the coat of arms of Canada.
All nations of the world at all times have used different flags for different tactical purposes. Those flags have been described as national, official or authorized flags or ensigns. Speaking before the joint committee on December 4, 1945, the Secretary of State (Mr. MARCH 21, 1946
The Address-Mr. Arsenault
Martin) declared that Great Britain at present uses over one hundred different designs of national, official or authorized flags or ensigns. Those who go to Montreal once in a while can see in the Windsor station over twenty-one designs of British flags. Prior to the last war France was using at least seven different flags which were entirely different from one another. Besides the tricolour there was the Tripoli merchant flag, the Algiers flag, the Tunis flag, the French Cochin-China flag, the kingdom of Siam ensign and the Madagascar flag.
To-day the United States of America are using at least six different flag designs. There are the stars and stripes, the President's flag, the United States union jack, the United States yacht ensign, the United States revenue flag and the Hawaiian flag. Although Hawaii is a possession of the United States, their flag has nothing at all of the stars and stripes in its design. Another example, is the island of Malta which is a British possession. They also have a national flag which has absolutely nothing in common with the union jack. As we all recall, that flag is the Maltese red cross on a white field. There are scores of other examples that could be given all along the line.
As do other leading countries of the world, Canada may use different designs of flags, either national, official or authorized, for different tactical purposes. Canadians could at
this time, on behalf of unity, take advantage of these exceptional circumstances and the great interest aroused by the choice of a national flag to settle onde and for all, not only this matter of the choice of a national flag for Canada but the whole question of our Canadian flag and ensigns. This should be settled by an act of this parliament of a free nation.
Since Canada is a member of the British commonwealth, united to her sister nations under the constitutional authority of the same king, I cannot very well see why anyone in this country could reasonably object to the full-sized union jack being officially recognized by this parliament as the official symbol of our partnership in the commonwealth, the finest example in history of mutual friendship between nations and one of the strongest means of maintaining peace in the world in these trying days.
Too much is involved to try to put forward any sort of narrow nationalism in the face of the distressful conditions that we find in the world to-day. Not only should we help to maintain the British commonwealth of nations, we should have a commonwealth of all the nations of the world based on the same principles of mutual friendship and collaboration. The union jack is here to stay, to stay as long as Canada is ready to share her obligations and the benefits of her privileges as part of the British commonwealth of nations. There is a great principle involved in this issue with far-reaching consequences which cannot be overlooked by anyone. As a French-speaking representative in this house from the province of Quebec may I say that Quebec will be the last province of Canada to pull down the union jack. Our religion, our language, our civil rights were guaranteed and granted to us French-speaking Canadians under the union jack. As the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) stated in the house on November 13, 1945:
It is under the union jack that the institutions of this Canadian nation have grown' and developed and have 'brought us to the point where now, and for a good many years now, the dominion is and has been an autonomous state subject in no phase of its domestic or its external affairs to any other authority than this Canadian parliament.
I notice that my time is just about up, but with the unanimous consent of the house I should like to finish stating my conclusions. They will take only a few more minutes. The province of Quebec also remembers, as much as any other part of Canada, those uncertain and crucial days of 1940 and 1941 when there occurred the collapse of France and of all organized armed resistance on the European continent, when the United States had not had Pearl Harbor and when Soviet Russia had not yet entered the war. Quebec realizes that we Frenchspeaking Canadians or English-speaking Canadians would all be slaves of Germany to-day had it not been for the three crosses of Saint George, Saint Andrew and Saint Patrick which were joined together and lifted proudly by Great Britain along with the dominions against the enemies of mankind,
As evidence of this contention and without any discriminating intentions, may I say that while the red ensign, the authorized flag of our merchant navy, is flown on these parliament buildings, the union jack, the full-sized union jack still unfolds itself to the breeze on parliament hill of Quebec only a few acres away from the very spot where 187 years ago two chivalrous and gallant soldiers, Wolfe and Montcalm, sealed the fate of this country.
Canada's constitutional position to-day with respect to Great Britain is similar to the position of Scotland with respect to England from 1603 to 1707. For over one hundred years the two kingdoms of Scotland and England were united under one king but had separate parliaments. For over one hundred years, from 1603, the year of the union of the two kingdoms under one king, until 1707, the year of
The Address-Mr. Arsenault

the legislative union of the two countries, each of fhese nations had their national flag but both nations used the union jack at the same time as the king's flag, the flag of their union under the same king.
To-day Canada is constitutionally an equal of Great Britain. Each country has a separate parliament but both countries are united under the same king. Each country has the same symbol of allegiance to the king, the union jack. Canada has an ofEcial flag, the union jack. Canada has an authorized ensign for her merchant marine, the red ensign. Canada now needs a national flag such as both England and Scotland had prior to the legislative union of the two countries. Therefore, I propose, as the only possible satisfactory and final settlement of the flag issue in Canada, the following, which will undoubtedly win the almost unanimous support of all true Canadians of whatever racial extraction or language:
1.	That this parliament of a free, autonomous and independent nation reconfirms the union jack as Canada's king's flag and as the official symbol of our country's partnership in the British commonwealth of nations.
2.	That this parliament maintains the red ensign in the functions it has filled ever since 1892 as the naval ensign of Canada's merchant marine, with possibly the coat of arms being replaced by the maple leaf.
3.	That this parliament gives to the Canadian nation a national flag, which will not be an English-Canadian flag, or a French-Cana-dian flag, or an English and French colonial flag, but an all-Canadian national flag.
Speaking in this house on November 13, 1945, the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) declared:
The purpose for which it is suggested there should be a distinctive national flag is to have a symbol that all Canadians can look upon as distinctively their own, not because they want to discard the union jack, but because the union jack is not distinctively their own and because they feel that their nation has now reached the stature in the family of nations that requires it to have something which can be regarded as its own.
On February 14, 1938, when the flag ques-tiontion came up in this house, the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made the following statement:
The use of the union jack on anything that is distinctively Canadian in the United States does not help to emphasize the individuality of this country or its distinct nationality; it helps to submerge them together.
The hon.. Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), speaking in this house on the same subject on November 8, 1945, said:

We in Canada have shared the union jack, and we shall always honour it as the symbol of much that is best and most precious in our heritage; but we have had nothing that has been peculiarly and indisputably our own, that would symbolize Canada, all of Canada and everyone in Canada. There should be something that all can see and look to with pride, as the symbol of this great nation of ours, to which affection and loyalty can attach, and which can become the sign of the unity and purpose that will make Canada great.
One final quotation. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), speaking in this house on November 8, 1945, said:
I wish to see Canada with a distinctive flag, and in my opinion the red ensign with -a coat of arms on it, which I would rather say nothing about, is not a distinctive flag. . . . The flag of the British commonwealth is the union jack, and we respect it, but I am pleased indeed to know that my hon. friends to the right are prepared .to recognize that the time has come when Canada should have a flag of her own.
Mr. Speaker, Canada is a free nation, just as politically free from Great Britain as Great Britain is free from her, and certainly more economically independent from the British isles than she is from us. Therefore a national flag for Chnada must not constitute the symbol of what Canada was when she stood as a colony under the supreme authority and jurisdiction of the imperial parliament, but of what she is to-day, an independent nation, a respected power amongst the nations of the world.
Like most countries Canada has a symbol which is recognized1 the world over as the expression of Canadian nationality. That emblem is the maple leaf. On this one thing we find the Canadian people almost unanimous, that the maple leaf must be given the position of honour in the proposed national flag if it is to be ad all-Canadian flag.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak as a private member of the house and as a member of the opposition. I have consistently supported certain principles ever since I came into the house.
First I wish to congratulate the government upon writing off the $400,000,000 owed by Britain to Canada under the commonwealth air training plan, and next I congratulate the government upon advancing a loan to Britain to facilitate the exchange of exports and imports between our two countries.

The Address-Mr. Church
I should like to say to the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Arsenault) and to the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacoihbe) that had it not been for the glorious young Canadians and young men from the other dominions who stood by Britain's side when she had to go it alone at Dunkirk and afterwards at Dieppe, we might have experienced the awful horrors of war on our own Canadiaji soil, the concentration camps, the whip, the gestapo police, the loud speaker and savagery-and the carting away of thousands of the people of Quebec, Ontario, and the maritimes as thousands were carted away from countries ravaged by the German war machine. Now is the time for cool heads, clear thinking, and plain speaking. There is * a great deal of kindness in this House of Commons. I found that out years ago when I first entered the house, but the time has come to pay tribute where it is due, to Britain for saving our shores from invasion.
Speaking of the glorious part that France played in the war of 1914-18 and of the tribulations which that country suffered and her triumphs I would remind the house that Mr. Churchill said that France will always be a great nation and ally of Britain, and we all hope that it will be restored very shortly.
I wish to congratulate the government on the appointment of that great *soldier, Lord Alexander, to be governor general of this country. In the session of 1943-44, in a debate on external affairs, I proposed to the Prime Minister that after a great war we should follow what was the custom in that great land to the south of us where, following the war between the north and the south, great soldiers were elected to be president of that great country, and that similarly we should appoint a great soldier to be governor general of Canada, and in that debate I proposed that either Lieutenant-General Montgomery or Lieutenant-General Alexander be appointed the next governor general of this country. I hope there will not be any departure from that principle of a great Briton being appointed, which has been observed since confederation. Appointments from the old land act as a system of checks and balances. It is a system -which harmonizes parties and eliminates party strife, and the various great men who have occupied the office have done a great deal for the welfare of our empire and of mankind.
I have referred in this house from time to time to the principles which I continue to support. As you know, Mr. Speaker, Christianity is part of the law of England, and by the Constitutional Act of 1791 it became
the law of Canada. Certain principles should be supported in these debates. These are some economic truths which should be an aid: To uphold the Christian religion and resist all attacks on it. Adequate security against external aggression and safety for our seaborne trade. An armed Britain forever aided by Canada. The maintenance of internal law and order, that all men may reap what they have sown. Impartial justice administered by a judiciary free from any interference or pressure on the part of the executive, and I want to compliment the member for West Calgary (Mr. Smith) on his able address last nigjbt in the liberty of -the subject. Sound finance and strict supervision of our national income and expenditure. Continuous and long-sighted development of our empire trade, without which Great Britain and her dominions will perish. The promotion of all measures which will improve the health, happiness, welfare and social conditions of the people of this country as a whole. Support of private enterprise and initiative as against state trading and the nationalization of industries. Go not with the multitude to do wrong. Always tell the truth to the people. You can ask a sacrifice of the people without fear, but to offer a bribe is dangerous. While it is not the empire's business to be the policeman of the world, it is equally not our job to be its governess. Trust the people and they will trust you.
I say to the government of the day, do not be afraid to tell the people that you have made a mistake. The Canadian people do not expect its leaders to be gods. Lastly, never legislate against human nature.
There are four cardinal principles which we in this country have forgotten, although I believe they are intimately connected with our greatest domestic problems of the present time. They are as follows: parliamentary reform, constitutional reform, cabinet reform and law reform. Twenty years ago they got law reform in England. In this matter we are twenty years behind the times. Long overdue is the consolidation of our statutes, which I have urged for a number of years, as also has the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) since he came to the house. The code was written in 1907. As the debates have shown, our laws need overhauling.
A day or two ago there was introduced into the legislature of Ontario a budget which forecasts a deficit of $21 million, and which is another evidence of the need of a new charter for the provinces. When all is said and done, such conditions were beyond the
The Address-Mr. Church

scope of the imagination of the fathers of confederation. The provinces were created, one might say, for political and not economic purposes. As I have said before, they are only a duplication of the municipal system. But if their powers and rights and privileges under section 92 of the British North America Act are taken from them by this parliament,' the time must come for writing a new charter. They are here now to stay and have a function and a duty to perform in confederation, and it is not right to take their revenues away from them and then expect them to meet post-war conditions. I look upon the province of Ontario as a forgotten child of confederation. Some years ago, together with my friend Mr. McCrea, of Sherbrooke, then a very much respected government member, I asked a question which was the subject of joint returns, which showed that forty-three per cent of the cash taxes of this country are paid by Ontario, and about forty-one per cent by Quebec, so that eighty-three per cent of the cash taxes of this country are contributed by the two industrial provinces. I have always been in favour of the principle for confederation, the old Cornish battle-cry, "Each for all and all for each." I believe that principle is yet sound. I never heard before 1939 the argument that the province of Ontario is living off the west; I am sure it is not right, either in the economic sense, the historical sense, or any financial sense The time has now come when something should be done on this subject and the government must find a solution of the problem in the coming dominion-provincial conference. Ontario needs active help and at once to meet her functions.
I should like to say a word in reply to those who raised the question of providing food for Britain. It is proposed that we should have . a much greater food production. I remember that in the session of 1938, three months before Munich, and again in the spring of 1939, when the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture were before the house, and I saw the war coming, and when the British Medical Association were meeting in London, I proposed that this country should establish underground food reservoirs to store our wheat, food and canned goods in the old country. At that time Canada had a preference for wheat in the mother country. Yet there were those on the prairies who contended that theirs was a free trade industry, that it was a north and south industry instead of an east and west industry to Britain and her allies. That was proven to be a fallacy. At the meeting of the British Medical Association it was shown that hard

wheat could be stored scientifically and kept good for ten years over there, and not the Canadian wheat bootlegged the way it used to be along the harbours of the seaboard on the United States side.( Had such war food reservoirs been established and wheat stored there, consider what the position would have been in the spring of 1940 and in 1941 when, during the great battle of thfe Atlantic, the mother country had only two and half weeks' supply of food. We abrogated the British preference foolishly on wheat by the United States treaty of 1938 and threw away our preference. I mention this to indicate what might have been done in view of the war, at a time when, I believe, we had half a billion bushels of wheat available a year, instead of paying an acre bonus not to sow it at all.
On this matter of food production I doubt whether the government has gone far enough. It is all very well to talk about summerfallowing and that sort of thing; the grain could be sown now and shipped next fall to the markets in Europe, where suffering is so intense. If we go into the production of coarse grains and turn them into pork it will be some time before the product will be obtained. I believe that my leader, the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Bracken), was quite right in calling the government's attention to that particular point.
I support this loan to Britain because it is founded upon a sound basis, namely on the exchange of goods and services in the form of exports and imports. It is not like the United States loam, which is simply an exchange of goods for gold or for debt. Why was that debt of Britain incurred with our great ally to the south? I was in Cleveland the other day, in Buffalo and in some other cities in the United States and I found out what former members of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation had been doing. Upton Close and others who think like him were before and for a year or two on the payroll of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation at one time, and I remember calling the attention of the government to the fact that the C3.C. were hiring aliens here to spread news unfavourable to this country and the empire and the cause of the allies. As a matter of fact, at that time the C.B.C. was one of the most mischievous institutions in Canada. It was sending out information which it had no right to disseminate. What did Upton Close say in Cleveland the other day? There appeared in the Cleveland Plain Dealer advertisements of his views for meetings, in which he said that the British empire is on crutches and is nearly at the end of its day. Similar views have been expressed by others. I have here reports of speeches made in the old country commenting on all this, but I will not take the time now to quote from them. I wish to protest against the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation being used in this mischievous way at a time when the mother country has suffered so severely. We find twenty-six thousand church and school buildings destroyed over there, while not a farmhouse, not a barn has been pulled down, as a result of the war, either in Canada or in the United States.
Surely we can pay tribute to the mother country for what it has done and not cavil about a measly loan. As a matter of fact, some of the best businessmen in the country, Liberals too, have pointed out that the loan to Britain is a splendid business proposition and should be extended. I believe it could be increased to two and a half billions over two years, and the other two billions could be taken
up by New Zealand and Australia, many of whose wonderful products have been displayed from time to time at our exhibitions here.
The Canadian people are long suffering, but there is a limit to their patience. That limit has been reached. As a result of mistakes made in the war and in the reconstruction period so far, they are losing their confidence in all governments. They believe that there has been overgovernment and overtaxation in Canada, and they are losing their confidence not only in the administration but in members of parliament as well. They are becoming critical of the work that is being done in the nation's various legislatures. The worst of it is that the public are not really acquainted with the facts in any situation that confronts them. They cannot get the truth and the whole truth concerning any problem that faces the governments of Canada. No; they have been blindfolded. They have not been given the real, actual facts. We have had a control system in this country throughout the war- we still have it-which has virtually made the work of the House of Commons unnecessary. We might as well have gone home and locked up the House of Commons, for in part the nation's affairs in the war have been handed over to boards over the head of parliament, over the law courts of the country, without any public regulation whatsoever.
There is now too much soothing syrup being poured over the radio by controls and bureaucrats. There is too much of that sort of thing being dished up and served for the purpose of making Canadians happy. There is no sacrifice that Canadians will not willingly make in this time of peace and reconversion, just as there was no sacrifice during the war which they were unwilling to make. But the people should be given the facts. There is a great deal of waste in Canada to-day. I have seen in our cities and towns in various parts of the country garbage collectors picking up half loaves of bread and all that sort of thing. There is too great a waste of food and something should be done about it, and I am glad to see the government starting a conversion and saving campaign.
I do not mind saying that in my opinion the government is taking a step in the right direction, but it should have taken that step long ago. I repeat, the people of Canada want to know the truth about the conduct of public business, and not necessarily the official truth. The fact is that we did not get the official truth about the spy business. We have always had spies in this country. I have seen them in Ottawa attending sport contests and regattas before the last war- Ribbentrop, Yon Papen and the like. In this

We have seen in the city of Ottawa a large basic industry doing more to solve the unemployment problem than any other agency, the business known as the embassy cure for unemployment. I do not know what they are going to do in the hot weather here if they all wear uniforms, swords, epaulettes and steel spurs; but I do say we are making ourselves ridiculous with all these Canadian embassies scattered all over the world. What do these men do? Well, the Canadian envoys make speeches all over the seven seas, and it is costing a great deal of money to maintain these embassies abroad.
That is something I should like to see the Conservative party deal with. I am a Con-
[Mi. Church.]
servative, and have never been anything else. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) said I was the only "true blue" left.
I have always been a progressive Conservative; but with all the principles I have supported from the time I was on the Toronto city council, I do not think I need call myself a Progressive Conservative. Let the Conservative party stand firm on the ground that the state exists for the individual, not the individual for the state; that state interference with the full liberty of the subject is an evil thing per se, the encroachments of which should be most searchingly scrutinized and resisted; that no government department, except where it enjoys a monopoly, can conduct business at a profit; that the prosperity of the nation rests on the enterprise and ability of individuals in free association to conduct their affairs with a minimum of regulation and interference; that capital and labour are partners and not enemies, indispensable to one another; that bureaucracy is the enemy of both and will ruin them morally and financially if they do not restrict its inordinate increase; and, finally, that what the Conservatives seek is the welfare of the whole community, and no sectional or class advantage.
In the debate last year, on September 11, 1945, I referred to the insistent demand all over the country that there should be some declaration of policy by the government in regard to its various control bodies, but I find that little or nothing has been done. At the present time all kinds of bodies are spending money like water, over the head of par-' liament. As I said in this house on September 11. 1945:
Every, principle for which the British nation struggled in the old land since the 17th century has been surrendered to the political caucuses. Parliament itself, which came into being to ensure that taxes shall be voted only by those who have to pay them, has become the institution through which those who do not pay them impose them on others.
I want to emphasize to the committee that powers of legislation older even than the right of taxpayers to determine the national expenditure have been surrendered, and if we are to continue this sort of thing the power of parliament will be gone forever. Whole spheres of activity, involving the livelihood of every man, woman and child in this country, have been removed from the jurisdiction of the law and of parliament and reserved for the determination of tribunals, irresponsible, irremovable, governed by no control and subject to no appeal, ...
I come from a very large taxpaying city. The working class have to pay a 12 per cent sales tax, and the burden of taxation is very heavy upon them and upon'business firms in the district. Some small business men have been put out of business altogether.
Let us stop feeding inflation by these huge expenditures. In Washington they propose to reduce expenditures by at least fifty per cent,

while we are increasing them by leaps and bounds. We should call a halt to this sort of thing. The trouble is that we are only holding a postmortem when we come to this house. I was glad to see the new auditor general's report, because three or four years ago I had a letter from Mr. Sellar, who at one time was secretary to a very good finance minister, the late Mr. Robb. I was complaining that he had not the powers of the former auditor general, John MacDougall, who would raise questions in the back of the auditor general's report, pointing out to parliament the errors made in the name of the state. We all know what happens to an individual or to a nation which goes on borrowing and does not keep its -finances within bounds. It becomes bankrupt. When you continue to spend more than you make and keep on borrowing money to make up the difference, you know the result. You know, too, that a big chunk out of every dollar a working man earns and spends is used to pay taxes. There is a sales tax on almost everything he buys, so that everyone should look at the way the government is spending our dollars. In my opinion the government should begin now to live within its means. During the war of necessity we spent huge sums of money; yet now, with the war over, the government proposes to spend much more -than in any pre-war year. Most thoughtful people believe that government expenditures are now far greater than; they need be. They believe that the government. like a family, should live within its means that it should not spend more than it takes in and that it should not keep going deeper into debt; yet that is exactly what is happening to-day. Our government is spending millions more than it takes in, and it continues to borrow or add taxes to make up the difference. That is the sort of money handling that causes inflation. Economy in government means money in your pocketbook. If the Canadian people will act to reduce government spending and take steps to increase -production, inflation will be stopped; and this is the only way in which it can be stopped. I urge this house to cut the cost of government, to eliminate all waste, all unnecessary services and postpone all expenditures than can be put off until our war bills are paid. Mr. Truman has adopted that policy, and I urge the government to start living at a level that we can afford to maintain. I wish to ask this question of this House of Commons, because I see a large number of returned soldiers here to-night as members of the house. What is to be the future position of the soldiers who are returning home to Canada? The trials and troubles and evils which brought about the second war are still with us; certainly at least the economic ones are: lack of housing; lack of employment; the return to old jobs; hospitalization for themselves and their families, and so on. Look at this housing situation. It brings to mind the situation at Bethlehem, where the Son of Man had to find housing in a manger. We seem to have made no improvement at all in our housing policy since that time. This matter has come before the house in season -and out of season, yet nothing has been done about it. I will tell you what is the difficulty in connection with housing. In 1935 the Bennett government at least did one thing; it appointed a committee to deal with this matter. There was a good deal of debate on a motion of mine, but that committee was appointed; it brought in a report, and the present government which came in in 1936-37, lent 89 millions of dollars for the construction of houses. I objected to the creation of a great housing department, and at that time labour and building materials were also scarce; yet under that policy the whole constituency of York West, the constituency of York South, the constituency of York East, and the northern portions of the constituency represented by the hon. member for Eglinton were built up by loans through the banks at three per cent by private enterprise. Down in one basement one could operate a building business in a residential district. Then, there was a little bit of an attic in another house about twice the size of the top of this desk with cooking stoves. That is what happens under this rent control system and irksome controls. I suggest that some of these housing controllers in Ottawa who sit in the swivel chair-

We know that by a process of lease-lend British bases were given up from Newfoundland to British Guiana and at other points for the use of fifty old United States warships, on a lease of bases. Half of those warships were useless. Many of them had to be taken to dry dock during the battle of the Atlantic. Yet all those are charged against Britain. Why should those bases not be charged up to lend-lease? A lease of ninety-nine years, practically freehold, should be charged up to lend-lease; that is where it belongs, and the ninety-nine year lease cancelled. I say that because of those fifty old ships only a very few had any value. Britain's battle of the Atlantic saved millions of people in America from axis invasion.
Something should be done about this. The freedom of the air and of the seas is vital to the British empire, more vital to it than to any other country or group, for the defence of the British empire to a 'high degree depends upon the unmolested transport of goods and passengers from one quarter to another.
The British empire is indeed the only political unit whose existence depends entirely on air and sea-borne traffic. Its over-dependence on foreign trade increases its need for command of the air and of the seas in certain areas and of the force to maintain that command. The United States could dispense with foreign trade to a great extent, without any great sacrifice or vital threat to its existence. China and Soviet Russia are similarly placed. But the British empire, western Europe, South and Central America are dependent upon foreign trade, and therefore on freedom of the air and of the seas.
I object to all this wild talk about internationalism. And what about the giving up of British bases on the seven seas? Russia was not in the war for two years. As a matter of fact, Russia had a trade agreement with Germany. The United States was not in the war for two and a half years. Where would we have been had we to share all British bases in the seven seas at Aden, Gibraltar, the Cape, Hong Kong and Singapore? We would have had to remain neutral, too. Did you ever hear tell of such a thing? Have we heard of such a thing as giving up British bases to foreign countries? The war would have been won by Germany. Give foreign countries all the raw materials we can give. But sovereignty?-no. That is one of the matters I have discussed before.
In conclusion, I wish to say a word about our old ally, Russia. Let us not forget that

she was an able ally of ours. We must remember what she did in this war. As Mr. Churchill said when he spoke at Fulton and Richmond, and1 again in New York, the hope of the world is that Great Britain, the United States and Russia may work together and cooperate for the good of civilization and of the world in general in peace as they did so well in war. Speaking last year, I referred to the league of nations. The only league of nations which was ever successful was the British empire. If we want to have internationalism, then let us start right there.	.
Russia believes that she is free to do as she likes in eastern Europe. She is not playing the game with her other allies. But I would ask hon. members not to forget that during the closing years of the first world war the Russian people were in the grip of a national revolution. The result was a humiliating surrender by the Russian forces to Germany at Brest-Litovsk, a surrender which would have permanently enslaved Russia to Germany if the United States, the British empire and France had not continued the war in spite of Russia's defection from the anti-German coalition.
At the present time she is not playing the game. But it is only a battle of nerves. I do not believe there will be another war. Russia wants security on her own terms in countries she has captured and invaded, and more room to reach the sea. She will not be happy until she gets it, and she intends to hold all she has obtained and reach out for more.
It will be recalled that on December 10, 1945, there was a meeting in Moscow between Mr. Bevin, Mr. Byrnes and the Russian officials. I believe they agreed to give Russia what she wanted in Japan; yes, five times more than she lost there in war forty years ago. Those two honourable secretaries agreed to support the puppet governments of Rou-mania and Bulgaria. All this was agreed without the dominions knowing anything about it.
Then, further, they agreed to everything that was done at Yalta. Who was present? It was Russia, the United States and Great Britain. They practically settled the peace of the world and the peace of Europe, even before the coming peace conference. It cannot be changed at that conference.
Then, what was done at Moscow? What did Mr. Bevin and Mr. Byrnes do? They went to work and left out France altogether, and instead of the big 5 -went back to 3 again -France should have the Ruhr valley ; she should have the Rhine, because twice in our 63260-11J
generation she has been invaded. Yet, as I have said, they agreed to recognize the Soviet puppet governments in Bulgaria and Rou-mania. They consented to exclude France from the treaty making in eastern Europe.
As Mr. Churchill has said, they did all this to aid Russia and to remove suspicion. True, Mr. Bevin did object to the eastern situation and the Dardanelles; but that had no effect at all, because Russia is bound to have authority and to give effect to her ideology. Communism will be revived by Russia in those invaded countries; there is no doubt about it. She is going to hang on to every foot of territory in Europe acquired with her army and navy. Mr. Churchill referred, when speaking in New York the other day, to the UNO or "you know who". We are at the parting of the ways. We may believe in miracles, but I think that Mr. Churchill deserves a great deal of credit for having placed the cards on the table and telling the people the whole truth and nothing but the truth of the aims of Russia. Petty criticism of that nature made by hon. members, just as that made a year or two ago by a newspaper correspondent of the expenses of our ambassadors, is a great disservice to the country. Canada is a great country emerging on the international scene and she must have a competent diplomatic service.
I saw the evolution of our diplomatic service during the years I was in contact with its members when on many occasions I accompanied the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe to imperial1 or international conferences. I think we have as good a staff of men as or in some cases even better than, the big powers. We should make life in the service more comfortable and free from worry and criticism. We should pay them more generously from the rank of third secretary up to that of ambassador. I hold no brief to speak for the personnel of the Department of External Affairs, but I think it is only fair to say the good I think of them especially when they have been doing such a good job.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is more responsible than anybody else for the

We know enough of these institutions to make it unnecessary for me to enter here into details of their functions and powers. I might be permitted, however, before I come to speak of what I consider the second way open to ensure the maintenance of peace, to give a few impressions I got while at the preparatory commission.	1
I have returned convinced that the delegates assembled in London were aware of the importance of making a success of the new organization and that they were all anxious to cooperate in the framing of institutions within which all nations may work to preserve their security and ensure better conditions for the world to live in
I am familiar, of course, only with the work of the preparatory commission as I was not present at the meetings of the assembly, and it is true that we were still in the elaboration stages, but that period was all the more important because then were drafted the regulations and were devised the means to put into effect the statutes enacted at San Francisco. It was constantly evident that any differences between delegates were motivated by a desire of each, according to his concepts, to ensure the security of his country and to prevent the possibility of peace being endangered by other nations. There were no sombre motives behind the objection of any country to the wording of a specific rule, but the eagerness to make sure that it would not work contrary to its purpose.
It would be wrong to assume, as certain people have insinuated, that the Soviet Union was aiming at rendering UNO inoperative when it pressed for certain amendments or objected to others. I am still convinced that it was as keen as the United Kingdom and the United States as well as Canada and any other nation to work out an instrument by which to render possible the putting into practice of the principles of the united nations charter.
The differences that exist between the Big Three and more especially between Britain and the Soviet Union, and that came into the open during the first session of the assembly and the security council, are an entirely different, matter, and I will touch upon them later in my remarks. They go far deeper than the setting up of the machinery needed for the establishment of a medium of intercourse among nations.
Somebody wrote in the press at the end of the first session:
UNO has deceived the hopes of humanity aspiring for a just and lasting peace; the result of this first experience is that union among the great powers has 'been compromised in London.
iMr. Picard.] ,
I think this statement is neither fair nor accurate. If there is a lack of union amongst the great powers, it cannot be attributed to the faults or deficiencies of UNO. It results from their lack of confidence in one another for the solution of problems which concern their vast conflicting interests.
I think on the contrary that there now exist well organized institutions which offer the best means devised to date to force the airing in the open of problems that may affect the peace of the world, whether these problems are presented in their true light or disguised in order to influence public opinion in other nations.
UNO constitutes the most advanced medium of regulating international relations ever agreed upon by the nations of the world. It is far from perfect, but we must give it our wholehearted support because it is one of our only hopes of succeeding to avoid conflict and therefore chaos.	[DOT]
Before I pass to the other part of my remarks, I should like to congratulate the Prime Minister on the decision which he took before San Francisco to include in delegations members of all parties. It is essential that Canada's foreign policies shall have some sort of continuity. If unanimous agreement cannot be arrived at in each party, at least some people of culture and ability and a sense of responsibility can be made aware of what is going on and can transmit to their political friends the motives and the reasons for certain decisions being arrived at. I think we may at all times, without violation of our convictions, develop a national point of view whereby Canada, like the United States and many ' other nations, will be able to present a united front in foreign or international affairs. One sees now in England at the foreign office a staff of men, directed by Mr. Bevin, consisting of people of varying convictions on political and social matters. I believe that Mr. Bevin has brought to the British foreign office, through his- vitality, his energy, his vast intelligence, new life and new "pep" to an institution which was venerable but which, I will not say was in need of, but would welcome new blood and new life, which he surely has the personality to provide. The British delegation was of one party only, the government party. The United States had with their delegation a prominent republican lawyer who, though he has never been in politics, is an important influence in his party. I think that was a really wonderful departure, and one which will ensure harmony if the practice is maintained.

The Address-Mr. Picard
UNO, Mr. Speaker, represents the legal way, the nearest approach to the ideal way of establishing conditions conducive to a lasting peace, but it will be made workable and its success possible only if the second way to ensure the maintenance of peace in the world is resorted to
No matter how well have been devised the organizations whose aim it is to preserve peace, peace will be secure only if and when the nations who have the potentialities to wage war are determined not to wage war. Peace, and I do not mean by that the settlement of all contentious or litigious questions between small nations, but peace that is the absence of war and the establishment of decent relations among peoples, will be possible when the big powers have ironed out their difficulties and not before. Let us not fool ourselves; the real difficulties are not those that are brought into the open. Britain and the United States are not offended at Russia's prolonged stay in Iran because it is a violation of the sovereign rights of a small country, nor is the anxiety of the Soviets for Greek democracy the reason of their protest to the council over British occupation in Greece, and the same applies to Indonesia or Syria and Lebanon. The game is a game for positions on the chessboard of Europe, and the pawns are the strategic points each one is anxious to acquire control of or not to lose the effective control of.
It is evident that the Bevin^Vishinsky duel, however it may have appeared in press reports, was not a personal fight. Both talked for mighty empires, which are, respectively, Russia the second and Britain the third power of the world, whose interests are conflicting on many points of the globe.
Ideologically the British socialists would seem to be related to the Russian communists in this, that both derive their collectivist theories from Karl Marx and Engels. However, everywhere throughout the world to-day the proponents of these two theories of social administration are strongly opposed to one another. British socialists have constantly resisted the infiltration in their ranks of communist sympathizers. Attlee, Bevin, Morrison, and before them Ramsay MacDonald and Arthur Henderson, have always opposed communism, and even more state capitalism, which would seem to be the system now in force in the Soviet Union.
This antagonism has nothing to do, however, with the present conflict. It results, according to me, from the fear and the lack of confidence in one another of two states eager to assure their security, one of which tries to capitalize
on its victory to realize century-old dreams, while the other tries to prevent that in order to maintain unchallenged century-old privileges.
Let us consider objectively the situation of the three big powers.
Britain has, over a period of nearly three hundred years, built the most powerful empire since the Roman empire ; it has been through its mastery of the seas the only world power up to the beginning of this war. Its security was guaranteed, first by its fleet but also by the maintenance of a divided continental Europe where no state could absolutely dominate the others. During the course of the last 150 years this security has been, menaced by the Napoleonic adventure, by the German ascendancy, initiated by Bismarck and culminating in 1914 by the imperialist ambitions of Wilhelm II and finally by the nazi onslaught. On these three occasions England mobilized all its energies and succeeded in preventing invasion and, through coalition with other states, in vanquishing her enemies.
The alliance with Russia and Prussia brought about the defeat of Napoleon at Waterloo; the Franco-British alliance, aided by the United States, Italy and Japan, won the first great war; the concerted efforts of Britain, the United States and Russia, assisted by all the united nations, have finally overpowered fascism and nazism.
After avoiding all these dangers, Britain succeeded, after each war except this one, in reestablishing in Europe conditions such that no state could by itself be a menace to world security for a time to come.
The establishment of coalitions or blocs of nations, in order to bring about a balance of power among the states of the continent, has been the best guarantee of Britain's security.
To-day, on the day following an Homeric fight from which she emerges much weaker and poorer, Britain sees on the continent a power stronger than herself, whose potentialities, despite its terrific losses, are not to bring quiet to the minds of British leaders.
During the course of the war, Britain accepted agreements intended to give Russia guarantees of security for the future which she judged indispensable. She accepted the Russian claims on the Baltic states and the settlement of the Polish problem. She recognized -that the Russian zone of influence should include Czechoslovakia, Roumania and Bulgaria. All this was probably dbne with reluctance and fear, but it had to be done. This fear no doubt grew when Yugoslavia and Albania came within the Russian sphere and when the Soviet ambitions began to resemble very closely those of Tzarist Russia.
The Address-Mr. Picard

The naval power of Britain, while guarding the safety of its communication lines, was the cause of its supremacy in the world and partly accounts for its wealth. She faces today a Russia getting more powerful. While she had always relied on the balance of power in Europe, she now foresees the Soviet Union dominating continental politics and approaching the North sea; she takes note of Russia's ambitions in the Mediterranean and the middle east and realizes that she may soon have a knife in her throat. This is why she appears determined to resist with energy any future Soviet expansion.
As to the Soviet Union, let us also consider her problem objectively. Twice during the last 150 years Russia had some of her provinces invaded and owed her salvation not only to her obstinate resistance but to the help received from maritime powers. Her security depends, above all, on her western frontiers. Russia has obtained and wants to maintain a sphere of influence in the states adjoining those frontiers.
' Whateyer may be the objections one has to communistic doctrines, one cannot deny that her past experiences justify Russia in ensuring that she has friendly neighbours. I cannot agree with the imposition by force of any form of government in a country, but these neighbouring countries were at one time or another during the war Russia's enemies, and as a winner she uses her rights to further her security and protect her borders.
The British seem to think that Russia's claim goes farther now than a mere anxiety or eagerness for security. There is evidently for a victorious state the temptation to live its dreams. Russia lacks outlets on warm waters. Her only ports free of ice year around are Murmansk on the Arctic ocean and Vladivostock on the sea of Japan.
The control of the Dardanelles by Turkey, the control of the eastern Mediterranean and of the Red sea by Britain, as well as the zone of British influence in Greece and Turkey paralyze Russia and prevent her from having, in all security, any access to the Mediterranean.
However, the Soviet Union has now by its influence in Yugoslavia and Albania a word to say on the Adriatic, and it might take away from the British, or render unsafe, the use of the natural harbour of Kotor on the Dalmatian coast.
The Americans appear less directly concerned with the European imbrogjio, but Russian power is not to reassure them. However, unless unforeseen events are precipitated, there are few points where Russian and

American interests are directly in conflict at the present time. But let us not forget that the United States have also considerable oil interests in the middle east and that their interests are tied up to a point with those of Britain, and it is highly improbable that they may remain neutral if war breaks out between Britain and Russia.
I may say, though, that Churchill's speech in Fulton, according to me has done more harm to the cause of British friendship in the United States than may be realized here. I was in New York at the time and came in contact with many people sympathetic to Britain who strongly objected to Churchill's speech. The general opinion on the street was: "Why should our sons die for the safeguard of British imperialism". And yet there is friendship for Britain in the United States. That speech was not timely or helpful. However, it is evident that, in the event of war, if the United States did not join Britain it. would face Russia the next day.
Soviet Russia dominating all Europe, succeeding to Great Britain in the control of the Mediterranean and the middle east and part of Asia, would be a terrific menace to the United States. The United States cannot remain aloof from the differences that crop up between Britain and the Soviets.
I cannot agree with the hon. member for Peel that Bevin and Vishinsky spoke clearly and put their cards on the table. If they did, they were double-sided cards and only one side showed. There may have been-strong talk in the council and blunt answers, but I do not consider this an improvement over the polished language of old diplomacy. Calling anybody a liar is not considered acceptable in good company. I cannot find it better, far from it, when said around the green tables of diplomatic conferences.
When I say that they did not speak clearly I mean that they have spoken for the gallery. They have enunciated great principles and have built a case to influence world public opinion, but they have not shown their real game. They have spoken of the defence of minorities and of their respect for democratic principles, but they have not spoken of oil, or of tin and rubber, or of naval bases or of lines of communications.
I say and repeat that the present fights in the united nations organization are fights for position and that the real problems are debated in the secret reunions of the foreign secretaries or the discussions of their experts, and the real fight centres around the terms of the peace treaties that are being drafted.

The Address-Mr. Power
The treaty with Italy is, according to me, one of the bones of contention, not as to what will be abstracted from Italy but as to how the partition will be done. The Italian colonies and the Dodecanese islands offer probably the most difficulty.
The region of Trieste-Fiume is disputed by Italy and Yugoslavia. I believe that Britain favours as a solution the establishment of an international free port in Trieste, in the manner of the Hanseatic ports of the middle ages, so that it may serve all central Europe. The Russians must insist on giving most of the region to Yugoslavia, their friend, or, in the event of a free zone being established in Trieste, will ask for one in Salonika, and the British will oppose it.
Italian North Africa offers more problems; the Soviets want a base in Tripolitania; they also want one in Erythrea on the Red sea, as well as one of the islands of the eastern Mediterranean. The most that Britain might be ready to concede is to internationalize Tripoli, like Tangier.
Then, there are the' Dardanelles. The Russians since the days of Peter the Great have aimed to get control of them. Mr. Churchill the other day, in New York, was ever so scandalized at the idea that the Soviets want a fortress to control the straits. He thinks it is enough to give Russia assurance that the Dardanelles will be free in war as in peace, under an international authority, and assimilates the Dardanelles to the Rhine and the Danube. The Soviets assimilate the straits to three others, two of which, Gibraltar and Suez, are controlled by Britain, while the third, Panama, is controlled by the United States. Would thd~ United States and Britain be ready to internationalize effectively these three gateways of the world? I doubt it. I am not saying this because I sympathize with coipmunistic views, nor because I want to defend Russia, far from it, but because I want to be objective.	,
In conclusion, I may say the ideal way to ensure the maintenance of peace would be through a world parliament, and failing this we have in the united nations organization a workable instrument.
Second, peace will be secure if the Big Three agree to talk plainly and compose their differences and have enough confidence in one another to accept compromises and adjust world privileges to the new relative status of power amongst themselves.
In common language, the question for the big powers is, do we share the spoils equitably and then, when our positions are strong and secure, do we become virtuous and live under 63260-12
international law as the reformed gangster often does in national life, or do we start fighting amongst ourselves as to who gets what?
Allow me to conclude on a more idealistic note by quoting the words of Nicholas Politis, former Minister of Foreign Affairs of Greece and one of the world's most famous international jurists, written in 1924:
We must now realize that the era of compulsory justice in international .affairs has started. After so many centuries of crises that at times divided them and at times united them, modern nations have definitely adopted the ideal of justice that, since so long ago, an enlightened humanity has strived without avail to attain. Slowly, timidly, they are bringing it about. The first hurdles have been cleared, another has just been undertaken.
The ultimate aim is still far away. There lies ahead a long road strewn with obstacles. Incessant efforts will be needed before the work can be completed.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to. speak on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I am breaking a rule of twenty-five years standing in my own political life. I do so because I fear that the matter I desire to discuss this evening may not be discussed later in the session, and also because I wish to take advantage of the kindly intimation by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) that he felt it was a salutary thing if his actions in matters extraordinary, such as those we shall discuss to-night, should be criticized in the House of Commons, perhaps in the view that should other occasions arise under similar circumstances the man charged with the responsibility of putting into effect legislation, procedure and methods similar to those which have been put into effect in these' circumstances, might hesitate to some extent before doing so.
I am fully aware that what I shall say tonight will not be popular either in this house or, where it means the most, at home. I shall be charged on the one hand with biting the hand that fed me, and on the other hand with being the reddest of red communist. I do not think I need say to this house or to those who in all probability will follow me and accuse me of being a friend of the communists, that by education, by tradition and by the religion to which I belong I have opposed nazism, fascism and communism; and it is because I fear that there is a tinge of some of these isms in that which I propose to criticize tonight that I rise in my place on this occasion.
Following along the lines of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the lines of the excellent discourse by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), I pro-
REVISED EDITION*
The Address-Mr. Power

pose to divide the matter which is being discussed into two parts, the international and the internal. Internationally I have the fullest confidence in our present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie King). I believe he will handle this matter without sabre-rattling, without war-mongering, with dignity and in the best interests of Canada. With regard to the Canadian element let me say this. I yield to no man in my hatred and contempt for those who may be found guilty of this the most heinous in the whole category of crimes. As the hon. member for Calgary West said, it is only by accident that they are not being accused of treason. They are being accused of something else; if they are found guilty will be found guilty of the lowest form of criminality, of having betrayed the secrets of their country to a foreign power; and the people of Canada will expect swift and exemplary justice to be meted out to them, as they are entitled to the greatest and swiftest measure of justice that our criminal code and out statutes provide.
I should like now to say a word with respect to the legislation itself. May I digress here to say that I freely acquit the Minister of Justice of any desire to mislead when he told the house there were no secret orders in council. I have known the Minister of Justice for twenty-five years. I have admired him as a citizen; I have admired him as a lawyer, as a man of honesty and integrity. I admired him fifteen or twenty years ago when, I think as president of the Canadian Bar Association, a citizen in no way involved in politics, he went out of his way, in an address which was often quoted in this house, to defend the liberties of the subject and to stand up for a constitutional form ,of government in this country.
Let us see what has happened in the way of legislation ; but first perhaps I had better read the magna charta. The most important and most famous article in the magna charta is this:
No freeman shall he arrested, imprisoned, dispossessed, outlawed, banished, or hurt in his person or property, nor will we-
Meaning the king.
an person or through our officers lay hands upon him save by the lawful judgment of his peers, or the law of the land. ... We will' to no one sell, deny or delay right or justice.
Let me place alongside of that the order in council, P.C. 6444 of October 6, 1945:
L The acting Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice, if satisfied that with a view to preventing any particular person from communicating secret and confidential information' to an agent of a foreign power or otherwise acting in any manner prejudicial 'to the public safety 
or the safety of the state it is necessary so to do, may make an order that any such person be interrogated and/or detained in such place and under such conditions as he may from time to time determine.
2. Any person shall, while detained by virtue of an order made under this order, ibe deemed in legal custody.
Those are the two documents, the magna charta and this order in council, which I think it is relevant we should compare. In his address on March 19, to be found on page 89 of Hansard, the Minister of Justice himself said:
I told them-
I think he meant the counsel for the commission.
-that if the order were one that was going to be made, then it would not be in that form; that I did not think in peace time it was proper that any member of the executive should have the kind of powers the order expressed; that I [DOT]thought no one should be detained, even for interrogation, without there being some form of intervention of the judicial authority; that we would act only ns if that were the provision, and that there would have to be a -recomemnda-[DOT]tion from some organ of the judicial authority to make me feel that I should exercise those powers.
Later on, in the course of the same address the minister repeated that he acted with a great deal of reluctance and hesitancy. I have here also the report of the committee on civil liberties, of the Canadian Bar Association. I am not going to read it all, but may I read this:
The affirmation of that right-
That is to say, the right of personal freedom. -has evolved some standard principles which have acquired almost sacred significance in the mind of the citizen:
(1)	The right not to be detained' >at the mere arbitrary will of the crown, or any government, or administrative authority;
(2)	The right not 'to be 'arrested, unless under the authority of a magistrate's warrant, issued on a' complaint diuly executed, and based on the ordinary law;
(3)	The right, when under suspicion, or arrest, or sentence, not to be coerced to give any information or evidence .against oneself, or to testify
in one's own case.
Those are the principles laid down by the committee on civil liberties of the Canadian Bar Association.
