It is to be found in the minutes of proceedings of the 27th annual meeting of the Canadian Bar Association held at Toronto on August 30 and 31 and September 1, 1944.
I should like to quote one more authority, which states:

The Address-Mr. Power
Now let us come to another point, which I wish particularly to stress. I refer to the right set out in magna eharta that no man shall be dispossessed of his rights without the lawful judgment of his peers under the law of the land; not the law as made by the governor in council, not the law ais made by some unnamed and as yet unexisting body, but the law of the land as known to everyone. It is an essential principle of liberty and freedom that the law of the land should be known, that it should be so known that every man as he runs may read. The. law should not be something which is to make its appearance in the Canada Gazette after some board or governor in council, not parliament, has passed a regulation; it is something that should appear in the statutes of the country.
That is the Right Hon. AVilliam Lyon Mackenzie King, Hansard, April 19, 1934, at page 2342. And with those authoritative statements I rest my case against what would appear to be a revocation of magna eharta, after 731 years of existence.
The point which I wish to make and which I consider important is that of the precedent which has been created in these cases. I am not sure about Great Britain. I am not even sure of the precedents created under the defence of Canada regulations made during the war. But I feel assured that no time in peace-time Canada have we ever had any such legislation as is contained in the order in council, parts of which I have just read.
The two hon. gentlemen who have spoken for the government in this debate, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice, are men of high reputation for integrity, for broad humanity,, for tolerance, for liberalmindedness and for a great regard for the personal liberty of their fellow citizens. As will appear from what the Minister of Justice has said, they have acted with deliberation, with hesitancy and, possibly, with a great deal of reluctance. No doubt they feel that they can exercise those extraordinary powers which were conferred upon them by the order in council with discretion and with the least possible injury to their fellow men.
But may I point' out that neither of these men has any guarantee of immortality. Neither is there any guarantee in our political life that the political wheel of fortune may not some day turn. And the numbers brought up on that political wheel of fortune may not always be the numbers of men in whom this country has the same faith and confidence as it has in the men who are now at the helm of affairs.
The hon. friend for Calgary West spoke about the book, "It Can't Happen Here." I think he was about to continue some discussion about that book when his attention was drawn to another point. Perhaps he was about to point out that in most totalitarian countries, or at least in the two of which we 63260-124
know the most, Germany and Russia, the majority of the people do not rule, or at least, did not rule. The majority of the people in Germany, we are told, were not nazis; and it has been repeated time And again here that the majority of the people in Russia do not belong to the communist party.
Nevertheless the men at the head of that party are the men who are in charge of those countries. They are in charge of the administration of justice; they are in charge of executive power. And it would appear to be from these men and from the kind of government they have that we obtain some idea of the methods which appear to have been followed) in this case.
"It Can't Happen Here", but it requires no great stretch of the imagination to paint what, to some, may be an extreme case, when misguided, intolerant, wilful and fanatical men might be at the head of affairs in this country, men who might confuse the security of the state with their own political security, men who might believe that their political opponents are plotting against the security of the I state because, forsooth, they are only opposing those measures which are being proposed by the heads of the state.
There have been harsh words spoken in the house and country about bankers, trust companies, cartels and monopolies. It might very well be that, through a turn of the wheel of fortune, the opponents of those who participate in monopolies and cartels might some day be in power and might believe firmly and conscientiously that the general security of the state, because of cartels with foreign nations, is seriously endangered.
Some of those very people who to-day applaud what is going on might find that they cheered to-day but they wept to-morrow. It is not without the recollection of hon. members-certainly not more than fifteen or twenty years ago-that a great American running as candidate for President of the United States was defeated because millions of his fellow citizens believed wrongly and wickedly, but perhaps sincerely, that his love of his country was vitiated by his allegiance to another country and to another ideology. Religious intolerance can bring people a long way. If religious intolerance ever came to the places of power and authority in this country I would not care to think of what might happen to those who opposed it. Precedents are dangerous things, and I regret far more than I can say that a precedent has been created in this case. These men could rely on the procedure and the approval by parliament, as
The Address-Mr. Power

parliament will approve, of the legislation and of the procedure which has been followed in this case.
I should like to have the time and perhaps the capacity to analyse something of the public attitude arising out of this event. I admit freely that in the popular mind the government is doing absolutely the right thing. I do not controvert or deny that for one moment; I only regret it. I feel that fifty years ago when we were closer to the great struggles which had taken place for human liberty or freedom it would have been more difficult for a government to proceed as this government has proceeded in this case. I wonder if the modem love of speed, efficiency, the cult of success in business, in politics, yes and in sport; the idea of winning at all costs; I wonder if that has not been so thoroughly impregnated into the thinking of our people that they are perhaps apt to forget what some of us believe to be eternal principles in their desire to see something done and done quickly.
There is the idea that we must fight fire with fire, that if these men had been in Russia perhaps it is more than likely that they would have been taken out and shot, and they should be here. We have fought a victorious war after four years. We have talked glibly of the new order which was to follow it, and it almost appears to me as though we the victors had taken on the manners and customs of the vanquished.
As to the accused themselves, I think I said I have no sympathy whatsoever for them, and I have not. But when I read the report of the members of the commission that some of these men, in admitting their guilt in giving the secrets of their country away, pleaded that they had another loyalty, a loyalty presumably, if not to another nation at least to another ideology, I wondered whether all of us are not to some extent responsible, not for these accused but for the fact that there are discordant loyalties in this country.
My hon. friend, the leader for the Social Credit party (Mr. Low), touched1 on the point when he said, or when I took him to say, that before we go too deeply into international affairs we should first try to become a nation on: our own, we should first try to develop a nationality of our own. I am perhaps one of those who smiled in a bit of derision at what was considered to be somewhat tawdry patriotism when reference was made to 100 per cent Americans. Perhaps it would have been good for us if we had tried to develop more 100 per cent Canadians. Some great

Irishman has said that if he were permitted to write the songs of a people he would not care who wrote their laws.
During the course of the war I had occasion to attend a large number of concerts, singsongs and so on in the camps of the various armed services. What songs did we hear? We heard "Annie Laurie", the "Rose of Tralee", "There'll always be an England". Did we ever hear any song about Canada? Have we ever tried to develop a Canadian spirit which would make those people stand abashed at the very thought of betraying their country? Our educational institutions are at fault. We are at fault in this house for developing loyalties, whether they be to other lands or whether they be to certain sections of our land.
Who forbade your bands playing "0 Canada"?
Not me.
One of your men.
That may be, and I shall be quite willing to answer my hon. friend at some other time.
I shall have an opportunity to do that too.

We have not developed as we should have developed a Canadian spirit. We have not developed it in our schools or in our colleges. Until such time as we do we cannot expect and we cannot hope to have in this country the right kind! of loyalty to our institutions and to our nation. When every man in this country has a loyalty to the country as boundless as are the acres of this country, when he is as much at home in Halifax as be is in Vancouver, in Quebec as he is in Toronto, when we have no such thing as sectionalism, then I believe it will be more difficult for wilful men to betray their country.
I should like to speak of one more aspect of this' discussion. I wish to refer to it from the point of view of liberalism, that is liberalism in the broadest sense, in the sense in which every political leader of this house has at some time or another and probably still is a believer in liberal thought and liberal principles rather than in the narrow sense of those who sit only on one side of the house; in the sense in which the hon. member for Calgary West is a liberal. I refer to liberalism which is defined as being a struggle for liberty, personal, civil, political, physical, social, economic, domestic, national and international. It is a struggle for the rights of the people against privilege and privileged interests and classes. The great victories of liberalism during the past century have been along the

The Address-Mr. Gauthier (Portneuj)
lines of constitutional reform. The Liberal party believes in individual liberty and in the rights of the citizen.	-
Amongst all the leaders of liberalism in this country there has never been any greater than the present leader, the Prime Minister of this country. I know he shares my views of liberalism for from long association with him I know his views on these matters. I know with what hesitancy and reluctance he must have acquiesced in what has gone on. I had hoped that he would have ignored that hesitancy and reluctance and would, when pressed, have refused to allow such legislation to be placed in the records of the people of Canada. He has taken a position with which I cannot agree. I respect his decision, as I hope 'he will respect my view.
As for me, brought up in an atmosphere wherein a framed photograph of magna charta was on almost every wall, accompanied with a warrant for the execution of Charles I, and steeped through my reading in the traditions of the martyrs of liberty and freedom, I cannot wish to turn back the pages of history seven hundred years and repeal magna charta. I cannot by my silence appear to approve even tacitly what I believe to have been a great mistake on the part of the government. If this is to be the funeral of liberalism I do not desire to be even an honorary pall-bearer at the funeral, and I do not wish by not taking part in this debate to give silent approval to the procedure which has taken place.

When I see you, Mr. Speaker, occupying the chair of the one we are agreed to call first commoner, you can readily imagine what memories are brought back to my mind and to my heart. You surely can guess that I see you as a young schoolboy, striving industriously to develop your character in the class-room, in the recreation and study rooms of that old institution, *>7enerable among all, the Quebec seminar}7.
It is because I was once a classmate of yours. We then found ourselves members of the Quebec Legislative Assembly, where we won our political spurs and where we had the pleasure and the privilege of sitting with a man whose fine sense of propriety we valued very highly. Since the beginning of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I have listened most carefully to speeches made in regard to the important problem with which the government was faced, namely the very contentious matter of the discovery of a spy ring in Canada.
There is one thing that I have particularly noticed. Not a single member of this house has any sympathy for these hirelings of the Moscow embassy or for the communist doctrine. Although no one has any sympathy for them, in the matter of technicalities, details and particulars, criticism has been levelled at the Right Hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and. at the Right Hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). No one has any sympathy for those spies but some feel that they have been treated too harshly.

It might please them if
we were to decorate those people.

However, I
know that some have been arrested and released on bail, and, after all, they were spies. In England, bail was refused1 to Dr. May. In Canada, things are different. As I am not a lawyer, I cannot discuss matters of technicalities but I know that when a man goes into the woods or the jungle, if he possesses the instinct of self-preservation, he will have brought with him some weapon to defend himself and when a wild animal springs at him to devour him, he does not argue, he does not plead for mercy, he asks no permission but he simply shoots it to save his own life. Is it what we are doing in Canada? This is what Canada is doing.
I cannot sympathize with spies. It may be argued that they have not yet been declared guilty. That is possible. But I will not believe that the Mounted Police, of whom so much good has been said in this house, have

recommended such a decision to the Right Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) unless they had proofs. That is preposterous. I repeat, we are now dealing with communists. We must not lose sight of the fact that the ultimate aim of communism is universal ideological revolution. Whether Stalin or others are at the helm of the Russian state, they are communists who hanker for the advent of universal revolution. They know how to go about it.

To -achieve its objective, the neo-messianic school to which Heine and Marx belonged strove to substitute materialism -for the -religious ideals of -a whole race.
